sens: Visible defect of the body, mark or physical imperfection
H8400.detail: 1. The word refers to a bodily imperfection, a mark that alters the appearance or function of the body — particularly an anomaly of the eye that hinders vision ("a blemish in the eye" in Leviticus 21:20), or any malformation that detracts from a person's presence. It is an imperfection that makes something or someone imperfect, in a sense "disfiguring" it.
H8400.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of defilement, confusion, or trouble. It is related to the notion of what obscures or tarnishes the physical integrity of a being. The root emphasizes the image of a mark or blemish that tarnishes the initial appearance.
H8400.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 21:20, in the context of the laws of holiness for worship. It is part of a long list of infirmities or malformations that disqualify a man from serving as a priest before the altar of the Lord. The term precisely characterizes a visible defect of the body that ritually disqualified, not out of malice, but because the service of worship in the Old Covenant required a physical integrity symbolizing purity before God.
H8400.portee: This list of disqualifications shows that the Old Covenant placed weight on the perfection of the priest's body. For today's Christian, it reveals the typical and transient nature of these ceremonial rules: Jesus Christ, the Great High Priest, has freed us from these external prescriptions. It invites us to understand how the Law was a "tutor" leading to Christ, and how grace receives us without the condition of physical perfection.

sens: Residues of cereal stalks after harvest or threshing
Material used in brick making
Fodder for feeding animals
What is light, insignificant, or worthless (figuratively)
H8401.detail:
1. Straw is what remains of the stalks of wheat, barley, or other cereals once the grains have been harvested. It is a waste of the harvest, but a useful waste.
2. In ancient Egypt, straw was mixed with Nile mud to make bricks: it strengthened the material and made it more solid. Exodus 5:7-18 recounts how Pharaoh deprived the Israelites of supplied straw, forcing them to procure it themselves while demanding the same number of bricks — a cruel punishment.
3. Straw also feeds livestock: in Genesis 24:25, Laban offers hospitality by providing "straw and fodder in abundance," and 1 Kings 4:28 mentions barley and straw provided for the king's horses.
4. Figuratively, straw symbolizes what is light, fragile, insignificant: Job 21:18 says that the wicked "are carried away like straw by the wind," and Jeremiah 23:28 contrasts the true prophet with the false prophet by saying, "What has straw in common with wheat?"
H8401.origine: The Hebrew word תֶּ֫בֶן (tèven) comes from a root that refers to the idea of what remains, of residue. In biblical Hebrew, it is the generic term for dry stalks after threshing, and it designates both construction material and fodder. The term appears consistently in the Old Testament in practical contexts: building, feeding livestock, or metaphorically futility.
H8401.emploi: The word תֶּ֫בֶן appears 16 times in biblical Hebrew, notably in two major contexts. First, the story of the bricks in Egypt (Exodus 5): Pharaoh refuses straw to the enslaved Israelites, illustrating oppression and the harshness of forced labor. Secondly, it designates fodder: Laban offers it to his guests (Genesis 24:25, 32), and King Solomon stores it for his cavalry (1 Kings 4:28). Finally, the word acquires symbolic value: it embodies fragility and insignificance (Job 21:18, Job 41:18), or the opposition between the true and the false (Jeremiah 23:28, Isaiah 11:7 and 65:25 imagine a world of peace where even the lion "will eat straw like the ox").
H8401.portee: Straw reminds the reader that God sees oppression and unjust labor: the Egyptian episode shows how He delivers His people from servitude. It also symbolizes vanity: what seems imposing or threatening (like the wind sweeping away straw) collapses before God's judgment. Finally, it invites us to distinguish the essential from the superfluous, the true from the false, in faith and word.

sens: Son of Ginnath, claimant to the crown of the northern kingdom during the period of Israel's division
Rival of Omri for the throne, whose faction was defeated after four years of struggle
H8402.detail: Thibni is a minor yet significant figure in the monarchical history of Israel. His name means "intelligent" in Hebrew. After the death of King Zimri, the people of Israel divided into two camps: one half supported Thibni as king, while the other half rallied to Omri (1 Kings 16:21). This political schism lasted four years, during which the two factions fought for power. Ultimately, Omri's supporters prevailed, and Thibni died, leaving Omri in effective possession of the throne (1 Kings 16:22).
H8402.origine: The name Thibni comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to understand" or "to discern"; it expresses the idea of intelligence or sagacity. It is a personalized name, borne by this sole claimant to the Israelite throne.
H8402.emploi: Thibni appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Kings 16, in verses 21 and 22. These passages recount the only documented period of his life: the succession of Zimri and his struggle with Omri for the crown. Thibni represents a key moment in the political history of the North, where Israel was torn apart before Omri's definitive victory, who became the founder of a new dynasty.

sens: Detailed plan or diagram shown to be copied or followed
Form or structure of a construction, object, or building
Sculpted representation or image, especially of idols or divine figures
Resemblance, aspect, or general appearance of a person or thing
H8403.detail:
1. The model is a precise plan given to someone to be executed exactly: God shows Moses the model of the tabernacle and its utensils, so that he builds them in every detail according to the specifications (Exodus 25:9). It is like a drawing or a description provided in advance to guide the execution.
2. It is also the structure, the concrete arrangement of a building or a finished object: King Ahaz sends to the priest Uriah the exact model and form of the altar he saw in Damascus (2 Kings 16:10). David receives from the Lord the detailed plan of the temple courtyards and all its chambers (1 Chronicles 28:12).
3. The word also refers to a carved figure or a sculpted representation, especially of idols: Israel makes a carved image, the figure of a man, a woman, or a beast (Deuteronomy 4:16-18), which is forbidden by the Covenant. Ezekiel sees idolatrous figures engraved on the walls of the temple (Ezekiel 8:10).
4. In a broader sense, it is the form, aspect, or visual image of a person or thing: the psalmist says that Israel exchanged its glory for the figure of a calf (Psalms 106:20), meaning that it replaced the worship of the true God with a bestial representation.
H8403.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of building, constructing, or forming. It is related to the image of something made, shaped, structured. It is a noun that denotes the result of the action: what is built, what is formed, what has taken shape. The word appears mainly in texts that describe constructions (the tabernacle, the temple) or visual representations (idols, engravings).
H8403.emploi: This word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in two contexts. First, that of sacred constructions: Exodus 25:9 and 25:40 use it for the model of the tabernacle that God entrusts to Moses; 1 Chronicles 28:11-19 uses it for the plan of the temple that David passes on to Solomon. The second context is that of idols and forbidden representations: Deuteronomy 4:16-18 uses it for the sculpted figures that the Israelites must not make; Ezekiel 8:3 and 8:10 mention it regarding the idols seen in the temple. Psalms 106:20 uses it to speak of the golden calf. The meaning of the word thus oscillates between authorized model (the divine plans of sacred buildings) and forbidden representation (the idols).
H8403.portee: This word shows that God provides an exact model for the construction of His sanctuary: He leaves nothing to chance; everything must conform to the plan He reveals. For the Christian, this teaches that true worship follows God's design, not human imagination. Conversely, the sculpted figures of idols remind us of the danger of replacing the spiritual worship of the true God with visible representations made by man.

sens: Place in the wilderness of Paran where divine fire consumed the rebels of Israel
H8404.detail: Taberah is a site in the wilderness of Paran where the people of Israel, complaining about the manna and longing for the meals of Egypt, provoked the Lord's anger. The heavenly fire ignited in the midst of the camp and consumed many, so much so that the place received this name which means "burning" or "blaze" (Numbers 11:3). It is one of the three major places of rebellion that Deuteronomy lists along with Massah and Kibroth-Hattaavah, symbols of Israel's unfaithfulness and the terrible consequences of its unbelief in the face of divine wonders (Deuteronomy 9:22).
H8404.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew תַּבְעֵרָה (taberah), which literally means "burning" or "blaze," derived from the root בָּעַר (ba'ar) meaning "to burn," "to consume." This descriptive name recounts the event that occurred there: it is because God consumed the people with fire that the desert retained this name of Taberah.
H8404.emploi: Taberah is mentioned twice in the Segond: in Numbers 11:3, where it receives its name during the judgment of divine fire following the complaints of the people against Moses and the Lord; and in Deuteronomy 9:22, where Moses reminds the new generations of this place of trial and punishment, so that they reflect on the consequences of rebellion. The biblical context is that of the wilderness journey and the crises of faith that marked the people since the Exodus.
H8404.portee: Taberah reminds the Christian reader that murmuring against God and His providers has serious and real consequences. It serves as a warning to remain faithful in the trials of the spiritual desert, rather than looking back to the temptations of sin. This name inscribed in biblical geography perpetuates the memory of divine judgment, inviting each generation not to repeat the mistakes of their fathers.

sens: Fortified city of Canaan, near Shechem, in the mountainous region of Samaria
H8405.detail: Thebez is a small city in Canaan located near Shechem (modern-day Nablus). It was fortified, with a wall and a defensive tower. It was there that Abimelech, a leader of Israel, met a humiliating death: a woman threw a millstone from the top of the wall onto his head, killing him instantly (Judges 9:50–55). The name likely means "brilliant" or "visible from afar," which suits a city built high on the rugged terrain of Canaan.
H8405.origine: The Hebrew name תֵּבֵץ (Thebez) is related to a root that evokes clarity, visibility, or prominence. The name recalls the strategic position of the city, built on a hill where it stood out in the landscape. It is a historical city of the Levant, mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in relation to the death of Abimelech.
H8405.emploi: Thebez appears only twice in the Old Testament, in the parallel chapters of Judges 9 and 2 Samuel 11. It is the scene of a key event: the siege of Abimelech (Judges 9:50) and his ignominious death (Judges 9:53–55). This story is recalled in 2 Samuel 11:21 as a precedent of humiliation in battle: a man killed by a woman at Thebez. These two mentions make Thebez a symbolic place of God's justice against the pride of Abimelech, who had massacred his own brothers.

sens: To shatter into pieces, to reduce to crumbs
To be weak or vulnerable, lacking solidity
H8406.detail:
1. To break into pieces, to reduce to crumbs: the word describes the physical action of breaking something. In Daniel 2:42, the feet of clay of the statue are "fragile," meaning brittle and easily breakable, unlike the iron which remains solid.
2. To be weak or vulnerable, lacking solidity: in a figurative sense, what is fragile lacks strength and risks giving way. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream, this mixed kingdom will not hold together: it will be divided and weak, like clay mixed with iron.
H8406.origine: The Aramaic word תְּבַר (tevar) comes from the same root as the Hebrew שָׁבַר (shavar), which means "to break." This root expresses the idea of rupture and fragmentation. It belongs to a family of words related to collapse and destruction: what is broken can no longer serve.
H8406.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:42. In this passage, Nebuchadnezzar receives the vision of a great statue whose feet and toes are partly of iron and partly of clay. The interpreter Daniel explains that this mixture makes the kingdom "fragile": it will be divided and without cohesion. The word expresses here not the action of breaking, but the state of fragility, the quality of what is brittle and can break.
H8406.portee: This image of fragility reminds us that human kingdoms and powers, even if they seem strong, often rest on unstable foundations. It invites the reader not to place their trust in the political forces of the world, but to see that only the kingdom of God, manifested in the dream as a stone that breaks all others, remains unshakeable.

sens: king of Assyria who conquered Israel in the 8th century B.C.
sovereign who deported the northern tribes of Israel
H8407.detail: Tiglath-Pileser (whose name means "you will discover the wonderful bond") is a powerful Assyrian king of the 8th century B.C. He invaded the Northern Kingdom (Israel) during the reign of King Pekah, conquering the border cities (Ijjon, Abel-Beth-Maaca, Kedesh, Hazor) and all of Galilee, then deporting the inhabitants to Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). King Ahaz of Judah, threatened by the Syrian-Israelite coalition, sought his alliance by submitting to him as a vassal (2 Kings 16:7, 16:10). Tiglath-Pileser continued his conquests by taking captive the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh, dispersing them far from their land (1 Chronicles 5:26). For Israel, his arrival marked the beginning of the end: it inaugurated the captivity of the ten northern tribes, who would never return en masse to their homeland.
H8407.origine: The Assyrian name Tiglath-Pileser comes from the Akkadian language. It designates a well-documented historical king in Assyrian records (reign: 745-727 B.C.), also known as Pul in some biblical texts (1 Chronicles 5:26). Cuneiform tablets confirm his military campaigns against the Levant and his massive practices of deporting conquered peoples, a policy of forced assimilation characteristic of the Assyrian empire.
H8407.emploi: Tiglath-Pileser appears six times in the Bible, always in a context of conquest and military domination. In 2 Kings 15:29, he conquers the cities of the North and deports their inhabitants. In 2 Kings 16:7-10, King Ahaz of Judah asks him for help against his enemies and accepts his suzerainty, which obliges him to see the altar that the Assyrian king built in Damascus. In 1 Chronicles 5:6 and 5:26, he captures Israelite leaders and deports entire tribes to distant regions (Chalach, Chabor, Gozan) where "they have remained to this day." These passages show that Tiglath-Pileser is the hand of divine judgment on Israel, using Assyria to punish the unfaithfulness of God's people.
H8407.portee: Tiglath-Pileser illustrates a major biblical lesson: the refusal to follow the Lord exposes God's people to pagan conquerors and dispersion. His invasion of the North marks a turning point in Israel's history — the end of the kingdom of the ten tribes — and reminds the reader that the promises of the Covenant only protect those who remain faithful. It is a catastrophic turning point that Jesus himself speaks of (Matthew 24:15) to warn his disciples.

sens: What one receives as good from a person — favor, gift, act of kindness
Generally something received without having deserved it — free gift from one who loves
The recognition owed to the one who has done good to us
H8408.detail:
1. A benefit is primarily an act of kindness that one person performs toward another, something good received. In Psalms 116:12, the psalmist asks: "How shall I repay the Lord for all his benefits toward me?" — he enumerates in his heart all the generous actions of God that have helped, healed, and saved him.
2. This word emphasizes that the good received comes from grace, that is, from the free goodness of the one who does it. It is not deserved in advance: it is a gift, a favor. God acts out of love for his people, not because his people have first deserved it.
3. The benefit entails a debt of gratitude. When the psalmist wonders how to repay the Lord for all his benefits, he expresses that one can never thank enough or repay enough for an act of grace. It is an opportunity to meditate on his goodness and commit to serving him.
H8408.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to pay back, to render." A benefit is therefore primarily a good action that one "renders" or "addresses" to someone. The noun "benefit" designates the act itself, what results for the one who receives it. It is a word that emphasizes the exchange — what someone good does for me, implicitly expecting my recognition in return.
H8408.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Psalms 116:12. It is a word of thanksgiving from the psalmist to God, which comes after he has described his danger and his deliverance (death and affliction in verse 3, then calling on the Lord and receiving help in verses 3-11). The context is clearly one of gratitude in response to God's interventions. The word appears in the plural ("benefits"), showing that there is not just one action, but an accumulation of good acts that God has bestowed upon the psalmist throughout his life.
H8408.portee: This word invites the Christian to look at their life and recognize the benefits of God — not only the spectacular miracles but health, family, forgiveness, protection of the day. The attitude of the psalmist — asking how to give thanks — pushes us toward active and continuous gratitude, less focused on what we ask for than on what we have received without deserving it. It is a posture of freedom and joy.

sens: To be overwhelmed, crushed by a force, weight, or affliction
To yield, bend under the blow
To die, be carried away
H8409.detail:
1. The verb evokes the image of a person collapsing or weakening under a weight that is too heavy. In Psalm 39:11, the psalmist says that he succumbs under the blows of God's hand: it is the physical and moral experience of one who can no longer resist the weight of affliction.
2. More broadly, to succumb means to yield before an overwhelming force, to no longer have the strength to hold on. It is to abandon resistance in the face of what crushes us.
3. The word can also carry the idea of being swept away, to disappear under the blow — to die or be consumed by violence or suffering.
H8409.origine: The Hebrew word tig·rah comes from a root that evokes the idea of fighting, contending. Its primary meaning is struggle, quarrel, or conflict between two parties. The Segond 1910 translates it here as "succumb" to emphasize not the conflict itself, but the fatal outcome for the one who yields: it is the effect of the fight, the collapse under the blows.
H8409.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Psalm 39:11). In this context, it designates the experience of the psalmist who, under the weight of divine punishments, feels his strength abandoning him. The biblical author uses this term to express moral and physical overwhelm: he no longer fights, he yields, he weakens. It is a powerful way to describe the disarray in the face of God's discipline.
H8409.portee: This verse invites the reader to recognize the real intensity of spiritual suffering: the psalmist does not pretend to be well. He cries out his exhaustion to God. For the Christian, this validates honesty in prayer: it is legitimate to confess to God that one is succumbing, that one can no longer go on. It is then that grace becomes possible.

sens: Hardwood tree with oval leaves, winged fruits in samara
Noble and precious wood for construction and ornamentation of the temple
H8410.detail:
1. The elm is a majestic tree with very hard and durable wood, featuring small leaves arranged alternately and characteristic winged fruits. It is a large tree found naturally in temperate and Mediterranean regions. The Segond translates the Hebrew word as "elm," although some scholars relate it more to other hardwoods like boxwood.
2. In both biblical passages, the elm always appears alongside other precious woods — cedar, cypress, boxwood — as a symbol of beauty, wealth, and permanence. In Isaiah 41:19, God announces that He will plant the elm in barren places to transform them into splendid gardens. In Isaiah 60:13, the elm is mentioned as ornamental wood for the future sanctuary, bringing glory and majesty to the holy place.
H8410.origine: The Hebrew word תִּדְהָר (tidhar) refers to a tree with particularly hard and beautiful wood. Although the exact botanical identification is debated among scholars, the Segond 1910 translates it as "elm" — a noble tree associated with strength and durability. In biblical Hebrew, this word does not have a known common verbal root; it designates this tree by its proper genus name.
H8410.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Isaiah, in chapters 41 and 60. In these two passages, Isaiah speaks of a future and glorious transformation: God enriches the desert with noble and precious woods to beautify His people and His sanctuary. The elm is never mentioned for its practical or common use, but always as part of a promise of divine transformation where sterility becomes beauty, and where the future temple shines with precious materials.
H8410.portee: These two mentions of the elm invite the reader to contemplate God's promises: He does not merely save; He transfigures and beautifies. The elm, durable and majestic wood, symbolizes how God glorifies His people and sanctifies His temple. It is a promise of hope: what is arid and barren will be filled with wealth and splendor through God's work.

sens: Continuity without interruption, constant repetition of the same action
Sustained fidelity, regular and uninterrupted devotion to someone or something
Constancy in effort, in service or in practicing a virtue
H8411.detail:
1. The word first evokes the idea of something that continues without stopping, that repeats regularly, like an unbroken chain. It is the notion of "always," "without ceasing." Daniel serves God "with perseverance" (Daniel 6:16), which means he serves Him constantly, day after day, never giving up.

2. Perseverance is a form of active fidelity: it is not a mere fleeting feeling, but a regular and lasting practice. The king notes that Daniel serves "with perseverance," like someone who maintains his commitment despite obstacles, and he hopes that this God, served with such constancy, will deliver him (Daniel 6:20).

3. Applied to divine service, perseverance becomes the virtue of one who persists in faith and obedience, without wavering in the face of trials or the temptation to abandon.
H8411.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root that expresses the idea of continuity, of something flowing without interruption. It is related to words that mean "now," "always," suggesting an uninterrupted duration. Its etymology paints the image of an action that prolongs, that persists over time.
H8411.emploi: This word appears twice in the Bible, only in the book of Daniel, in chapters 6:16 and 6:20. Both occurrences are identical and form a pair: they show the pagan king, Darius, observing Daniel's fidelity to his God. Daniel does not serve God intermittently or hesitantly, but "with perseverance" — that is, regularly, unwaveringly. The context of the lion's den emphasizes how remarkable this perseverance is: despite the king's decree prohibiting any prayer, Daniel did not stop serving his God. It is this continuity of faith that the text is interested in.
H8411.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that true faith is not a one-time adherence, but a lasting commitment. Serving God is not a matter of moments of enthusiasm, but of daily constancy. Daniel's example shows that such perseverance, even in adversity, is what pleases God and opens His heart to liberate and defend those who remain faithful to Him. It is a call to continuous fidelity rather than spectacular perfection.

sens: Fortified city in the Syrian desert that Solomon built after the conquest of Hamath-Zobah
H8412.detail: 1. Thadmor is a city built by King Solomon in the desert, between Damascus and the Euphrates, to consolidate his empire. Its Hebrew name evokes the palm tree (tadmor), which grows in desert oases: the city was a center for supply and trade along trade routes (1 Kings 9:18). It also served as a strategic stronghold, as Solomon built it after conquering Hamath-Zobah to the north (2 Chronicles 8:4). Thadmor became famous under the later reign of Queen Zenobia (3rd century), but the Bible only mentions its foundation by Solomon.
H8412.origine: The Hebrew name תַּדְמֹר (tadmor) literally means "palm tree." It also appears in the form תָּמָר (tamar), which refers to the date palm. This root evokes the image of the prosperous palm in the arid desert, a symbol of life and fertility where water springs forth. The name reflects the geography and ecology of the place: an oasis where palm trees allowed human life.
H8412.emploi: Thadmor appears twice in the Bible, always in connection with Solomon. In 1 Kings 9:18, it is mentioned among the "store cities" that the king built to stock food, weapons, and materials. In 2 Chronicles 8:4, the same event is reported: Solomon built Thadmor "in the desert" and surrounded it with "cities serving as storehouses" in Hamath. These two passages emphasize its logistical and military role: it was a strategic and economic hub of Solomon's vast empire, which extended from Egypt to Mesopotamia.

sens: Chief of nomadic peoples in the time of the Patriarchs
Ally of Kedorlaomer in a coalition of four kings
H8413.detail: Tideal is a king mentioned twice in the account of Genesis 14, where Abraham intervenes in a war between kings. He is referred to as "king of Gojim" (that is, king of nations or peoples), suggesting that he commanded various nomadic tribes rather than a fixed territory. He and three other kings — Kedorlaomer of Elam, Amraphel of Shinar, and Arioch of Ellasar — formed a military alliance that had subdued the local kingdoms before being confronted by Abraham's response.
H8413.origine: The name Tideal means "great son" (Hebrew "thi" = great and "dal" = son). It is unclear whether this figure is historical or legendary; no source outside the Bible mentions him with certainty. His name and title reflect the patriarchal era and the mobile political structures of the ancient Near East.
H8413.emploi: Tideal appears only twice in the Bible, both in Genesis 14, in verses 1 and 9. He is presented as one of the four allied kings who had subdued five kingdoms in the region of the Dead Sea. After Kedorlaomer captured Lot, Abraham's nephew, Tideal is mentioned again when Abraham prepares the counterattack against this coalition. The context shows that he was a powerful military leader, allied with recognized kings from distant empires.
H8413.portee: This account illustrates how Abraham, though a foreigner and without a kingdom, dared to rise against a powerful international coalition to rescue his relative. The presence of Tideal reminds us that God protects His people against seemingly overwhelming forces.

sens: Absence of form, structure, or defined contours
Void, absence of substance or reality
Desert, wilderness, barren and desolate place
Nothingness, that which is vain or without value
Chaos, primordial confusion
H8414.detail:
1. The formless refers to that which has no visible form or clear contours. At the very beginning of creation, the earth was "formless and empty" (Genesis 1:2): a mass without structure, before God ordered this chaos by separating light, sky, earth, and waters.
2. The word expresses total absence: that which is devoid of any reality or substance. The idols of false gods are of "nothingness" (Isaiah 41:29), meaning they have no real power against the living God.
3. Applied to places, it describes an arid desert, a barren and uninhabited space. The caravans "sink into the desert" (Job 6:18) and perish, lacking a reference point or water.
4. On a moral and spiritual level, it signifies futility or vanity. Seeking God "in vain" (Isaiah 45:19) means seeking Him without sincerity or result.
5. The word finally evokes primordial chaos, the state of non-being prior to ordered creation. God "did not create [the earth] to be empty" (Isaiah 45:18), but to be inhabited and organized.
H8414.origine: The Hebrew word תֹּהוּ comes from a root expressing absence and confusion. It is often paired with בֹּהוּ (bohu), a synonymous word for void, to intensify the idea of complete desolation. The term primarily appears in poetic and prophetic texts: Isaiah frequently uses it to describe future devastation or the ineffectiveness of false gods. Its basic image is that of a space without structure, without limits, without reference points — the opposite of created order.
H8414.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in the prophets (especially Isaiah, 10 times) and the Psalms. Its first use, in Genesis 1:2, establishes its fundamental meaning: the formless state of the world before creation. Job uses it for the desert (6:18; 12:24), a symbol of perdition. Isaiah applies it in three contexts: the primordial earth (45:18), the future judgment that returns the world to chaos (24:10; 34:11), and the futility of idols or wicked works (41:29; 44:9; 49:4). Psalm 107:40 describes men lost in the desert, an image of divine abandonment. The word nuances between initial cosmic chaos, devastation, and spiritual futility.
H8414.portee: This word reminds the believer that only God creates order and meaning. The "formless" chaos of Genesis 1:2 shows that creation was not natural or eternal, but the work of divine will. Applied to idols or wicked works, it teaches that everything opposing God or built without Him is "nothingness" — an apparent reality but without true substance. This word thus invites one to place their trust not in themselves or in illusions, but in God alone, the source of all form, meaning, and lasting reality.

sens: The underground waters or deep springs that burst forth from the earth
The ocean, the sea, or large bodies of water
The abyss, the bottomless pit, the terrifying void
The grave, the subterranean depths where the dead rest
Danger, perdition, misfortune that engulfs
H8415.detail:
1. The underground waters or deep springs that burst forth from the earth: in the Old Testament, the underground waters sustain all that lives — springs, rivers, rains. When Genesis speaks of "the abyss" at the beginning, it evokes these reservoirs hidden beneath the earth, from which life springs forth (Genesis 1:2; Proverbs 8:27 describes God tracing a circle "on the surface of the abyss").
2. The ocean, the sea, or large bodies of water: the word also denotes the seas and visible waves, often in violent motion. At the Red Sea, the "waves" rise like a wall (Exodus 15:8), or the waters harden like stone (Job 38:30).
3. The abyss, the bottomless pit, the terrifying void: the abyss evokes the unknown, the unfathomable, chaos. God masters this abyss: He "restrains" the ocean (Psalms 33:7), He "divides" it during the crossing of the Red Sea (Isaiah 51:10).
4. The grave, the subterranean depths where the dead rest: the abyss also symbolizes hell, the underground regions of death. The psalmist pleads with God: "You will bring us up from the depths of the earth" (Psalms 71:20), meaning from the realm of the dead.
5. Danger, perdition, misfortune that engulfs: when a ship sinks, when one goes through a storm, one "descends into the abyss" — the abyss becomes an image of extreme peril and distress (Psalms 107:26).
H8415.origine: The Hebrew word תְּהוֹם (tehom) originally designates the primordial waters, this great reservoir of chaotic water that existed before creation. It derives from a root that evokes the idea of "depth" and "vastness." In ancient Near Eastern religions, neighboring peoples spoke of a primordial deity of chaotic waters; the Bible adopts the word but desacralizes it: the abyss is not a god, but the creation of God, subject to His order. The word hardly reappears in the Greek New Testament, replaced by other terms.
H8415.emploi: The word appears 35 times in Hebrew, mainly in poetic books (Psalms, Job, Proverbs) and in creation or deliverance narratives. In Genesis 1:2, it describes the primordial waters before God brings order. In Exodus 15 and Isaiah 51, it symbolizes the Red Sea that God divides to save Israel — the abyss thus becomes an image of the peril from which God rescues us. In the Psalms, believers "descend" into the abyss in times of distress (Psalms 107:26), and then God "brings them up." In Job and Proverbs, the abyss is the unfathomable, that which escapes human wisdom. The word thus retains its concrete meaning (the waters) but takes on a spiritual significance: the abyss is everything that threatens, engulfs, crushes — and from which only God frees us.
H8415.portee: The word abyss invites the believer to measure two realities. First, the immensity and mystery of divine creation — the abyss reminds us that we live above an unfathomable universe, created and mastered by God. Secondly, in the face of the perils and misfortunes that engulf us, the abyss becomes a powerful image of our distress — but also of our expectation of salvation. For the Bible shows that God "brings up" His own from the abyss (Psalms 71:20): it is a promise of deliverance from misfortune and death.

sens: Expression of admiration and gratitude towards God
Song or hymn addressed to God to celebrate His greatness
Public and collective act of glorification
Honor, glory, or renown attached to someone or something
Praise required or deserved by the qualities and acts of God
H8416.detail:
1. Praise is primarily the expression of the heart that admires and thanks God for who He is and what He does. It is a personal act of worship and acknowledgment: in Psalms 22:26, the psalmist says, "You will be the object of my praise in the great assembly," showing that praise is what we offer to God when we truly recognize Him.
2. Praise can take the form of a song or hymn, a musical composition intended to celebrate God. Psalms 149:1 commands: "Sing to the Lord a new song! Sing His praises in the assembly of the faithful," showing that praise is sung in community.
3. Praise is also a collective and public act, an event where the people gather to glorify God together. Psalms 106:12 recounts how the people "sang His praises" after believing God's words, showing that praise unites the people in faith.
4. The word also refers to the glory, honor, or renown that someone or something possesses. In Isaiah 61:11, God will cause "salvation and praise to spring up before all nations," signifying that His glory and honor will extend everywhere.
5. Finally, praise is what is due to God, what His infinite qualities, holiness, and wonderful works deserve. Exodus 15:11 asks: "Who is like You, majestic in holiness, worthy of praise?" showing that God alone deserves absolute praise.
H8416.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to praise" or "to shine," evoking the idea of making bright or radiant what is praised. Praise is what makes someone's reputation or glory shine. The word belongs to the family of verbs related to singing and celebration. It is a specifically Hebrew word to express a religious act of acknowledgment towards God.
H8416.emploi: The word praise appears 57 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms and the prophets. In the Psalms (over 30 occurrences), praise is presented as one of the highest activities of the believer: the psalmists describe praise as a continual, spontaneous act that springs from a grateful heart. In Isaiah and Jeremiah, praise becomes a prophetic issue: God promises that His praise will rise among the nations (Isaiah 42:10, 43:21), or that His praise will extend over the entire earth (Jeremiah 33:9). The word signifies sometimes the action of praising, sometimes the fruit of that action (the glory acquired), sometimes the songs themselves. Its theological scope grows throughout the books: what begins as a personal act of acknowledgment becomes a cosmic event of divine glorification.
H8416.portee: For the Christian, praise is not a burdensome obligation, but the very breath of faith. Recognizing that God alone deserves praise restores the proper hierarchy to life: God at the center, created things in their place. Praise unites the believer with the great assembly of the faithful, past and future, and associates them with God's eternal glory. It is also a spiritual weapon: singing praise is affirming faith when doubt looms, it is witnessing God's victory over opposing powers.

sens: Lack of wisdom and reason
Error in judgment or action
State of mental derangement
H8417.detail:
1. The word denotes the absence of wisdom or discernment in thought and actions — the inability to see and do good. In Job 4:18, Bildad declares that God "finds folly among His angels": even celestial beings can lack wisdom before God, showing that foolishness is a failure of judgment, a deviation from righteousness.

2. More broadly, it is a serious error in conduct or decision, a form of blindness that leads one to act against their interest or against God's will — which makes the wise different from the fool in the eyes of the Bible.
H8417.origine: The Hebrew word תׇּהֳלָה (tohola) comes from a root evoking the idea of being mistaken, deviating, or going astray. It expresses the image of a mental deviation: not the furious madness, but the error of direction, the wrong choice of one who has not been able to see the path of wisdom. In Hebrew thought, foolishness is the opposite of hokma (wisdom), that discernment which allows one to understand and obey God.
H8417.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 4:18. It is found in the speech of Bildad, one of Job's friends, who asserts that even angels are not exempt from fault or folly in God's eyes. The usage is classic: it denotes a moral or intellectual failure, a lack of insight in the face of divine justice. In the context of the book of Job, this term emphasizes the idea that human wisdom is fragile and that only God is truly wise.
H8417.portee: This word reminds the reader that true wisdom is not a guaranteed possession, but a gift that requires remaining attentive to God. Foolishness does not necessarily mean madness, but the wandering of one who believes they can act without submitting to divine wisdom. For a Christian, this invites seeking true wisdom from God rather than relying on one's own judgment.

sens: Line of people moving together in an organized order
Solemn or ceremonial parade
March in a procession during a religious celebration
H8418.detail:
1. A procession is a group of people moving together in an orderly manner, following a determined path. The word literally denotes the way in which a line sets in motion and progresses. In Nehemiah 12:31, after the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem, Nehemiah organizes a solemn event: he forms two great choirs of singers and priests who walk together on the wall, each in a different direction, to consecrate the walls. This procession is not just a simple movement, but a public and orderly act intended to honor God.
2. The word evokes the image of a procession setting out: the participants advance according to an established order, often in a religious or civil procedure. In the context of Nehemiah, the two choirs do not walk randomly, but "in march" — that is, in a structured procession — on the right side of the wall.
H8418.origine: The Hebrew word תַּהֲלוּכָה (tahaloukah) is derived from the root הלך (halak), which means "to walk" or "to go." This basic root expresses the physical movement of feet. The suffix makes the word more abstract: it denotes less the action of walking than the organized manner in which one walks together, that is, the procession itself as an ordered procession.
H8418.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:31. It describes the crucial moment when the Jewish people, after completing the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem, organize a dedication ceremony. Nehemiah forms two choirs (groups of singers and priests) who ascend the wall and set out in procession: one goes to the right towards the dung gate, while the other likely goes to the left. It is a religious act intended to sanctify the accomplished work and to give thanks to God for the restoration of the walls.
H8418.portee: This procession illustrates how the people of God celebrate their victories and restorations by associating organized movement (the procession), worship (the choirs and priests), and public joy. It shows that faith is not only internal: it is expressed through visible and ordered acts, by which the community walks together under God's blessing. For the Christian reader, it is an image of the people of God progressing with order and joy in fulfilling their commitments to the Lord.

sens: Character of what is twisted, distorted, diverted from its proper orientation
Moral disposition to distort good into evil, to pervert just order
Word or action that expresses this calculated malice
H8419.detail:
1. The word first evokes the image of the twisted, the distorted — something that has been deviated from its natural form or direction. This is why the Bible speaks of "the perverse mouth" (Proverbs 8:13): a mouth that distorts words from their true meaning, twisting them to deceive.
2. On a moral level, perversity denotes this deliberate intention to do evil — not out of impulse, but through a kind of calculated system. Proverbs 6:14 illustrates this well: "Perversity is in his heart, he meditates evil all the time": it is a thoughtful malice, a heart disposed to invent evil.
3. Perversity concretely expresses itself in deceptive words or harmful actions. Proverbs 2:12 speaks of one who "utters perverse speech": treacherous words, calculated to mislead. This is why Proverbs 10:31 announces that "the perverse tongue will be cut off" — it cannot endure against God's order.
H8419.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that literally means "to turn, to overturn." It belongs to the family of words denoting diversion, twisting, overturning of the good order. The central image is that of something that has been turned around, inverted, turned upside down — what was straight becomes twisted. Perversity is therefore the result of a moral twisting action: taking what is just and distorting it.
H8419.emploi: The word appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the book of Proverbs (seven occurrences), which deals with wisdom and folly. It qualifies either a person or their heart (Deuteronomy 32:20: "They are a perverse generation"), or specifically deceptive speech — "the perverse mouth," "the perverse tongue." Proverbs shows that perversity is a trait of the wicked who "delight in doing evil" (Proverbs 2:14): it is not a temporary weakness, but a deliberate choice, rooted in the heart. The contrast with the words of the righteous (Proverbs 10:31) emphasizes that wisdom and perversity are two radically opposed paths.
H8419.portee: For the believer, this word reveals that evil is not always an impulsive act: it can be a cultivated, thoughtful intention, "meditated." Recognizing perversity for what it is — a deliberate twisting of good — helps not to be seduced by flattering or deceptive words. It also invites introspection: the human heart, without God's wisdom, naturally tends toward this inversion of values. This is why Proverbs often return to the love of wisdom and the fear of the Lord.

sens: Visible sign drawn or engraved on something or someone
Seal or signature attesting the authenticity of a document
Mark of distinction or divine protection against judgment
H8420.detail:
1. A mark is primarily a visible sign, a distinct trace placed on an object or a person. In Ezekiel 9:4, the Lord commands the prophet to make a mark on the foreheads of those who sigh over the abominations of Jerusalem: it is a concrete, visible mark that identifies.
2. The word also refers to a signature or seal that authenticates a written document. When Job declares in 31:35, "Here is my defense, signed," he speaks of a mark, a signature affixed to his writing to make it official and authentic — just as one signs a document today.
3. The mark can be a sign of divine protection or distinction. Those who bear the mark in Ezekiel 9:6 are spared by the destroying angels: the mark protects them from the judgment that strikes the rest of the city. It is a distinction that saves.
H8420.origine: The Hebrew word tav means primarily "sign" or "mark," and it is related to the idea of making a trace, marking or signing. It comes from a root that expresses the action of leaving an imprint or a visible sign. The tav was also the last letter of the ancient Hebrew alphabet, often used as a signature or personal mark. In biblical contexts, this word carries the image of identification and belonging marked visibly.
H8420.emploi: The word tav appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 31:35, it refers to Job's signature affixed to his defense writing — an act of authentication. In the two passages of Ezekiel 9 (verses 4 and 6), it takes on a major theological dimension: God commands the prophet to mark the foreheads of the faithful who sigh over the sins of Jerusalem, and this mark protects them from the destruction that will strike the rest of the city. The mark thus becomes a sign of salvation and divine distinction, separating the elect from judgment.
H8420.portee: This divine mark in Ezekiel reveals that God knows His faithful and personally protects them amid the judgment that strikes injustice. For the Christian, it evokes the idea that God "marks" those who belong to Him, distinguishing and preserving them. It is a call to sigh over sin and seek the protection of the Lord: those who pray and depend on God receive His mark, His seal of salvation.

sens: To go back to a place from which one has departed
To regain a faculty or state that one had lost
To restore, return, give back to someone
To give a response
H8421G.detail:
1. To return primarily means to physically go back to the starting point or to a previous situation: it is the reverse movement of a departure or separation. In Daniel 4:34, Nebuchadnezzar says that his reason "returned" to him, meaning that after his madness he regained the ability to think and understand.
2. The word also expresses the return of a capacity or quality that one had temporarily lost: reason, strength, consciousness. Daniel 4:36 confirms this meaning when it recounts that "my reason returned to me" and that "the glory of my kingdom" and its "splendor" were restored to him.
3. To return can also mean to give something back to someone, to restore what belongs to them: it is the action of one who puts things back in place. This meaning appears in Daniel 4:36 where his greatness is "returned" to him.
4. In a dialogue context, the word can mean to respond, to give an answer to the one who has spoken to you.
H8421G.origine: The Hebrew word tuv comes from a root that expresses the idea of return, of a movement of reversion. It is constructed in two main forms: the P'al form (the simple return) and the Aphel form (to make return, restore, give back). This grammatical structure reflects two aspects of the same movement: the natural return and the action of bringing back. The root evokes the image of turning around, of retracing one's steps.
H8421G.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears twice in Daniel 4, in verses 34 and 36, in the context of Nebuchadnezzar's dream and his restoration. In both cases, the king speaks of the return of his reason after a period of madness sent by God. In verse 34, it is the first mention of this return: "my reason returned to me." In verse 36, the word reappears to describe the complete return of his power and splendor. The context shows that this "return" is not a simple natural event, but a restoration granted by God Himself, marking the end of the king's punishment and his reconciliation with the Most High.
H8421G.portee: This word teaches that God is the master of restorations and returns. In the story of Nebuchadnezzar, the return of his reason and power does not depend on himself, but on divine grace. For the Christian reader, this text reminds us that it is God alone who can bring us back to Him and restore us after a fall or trial. The "return" is thus an act of mercy, not mere causality.

sens: To return something to its owner or to its original place
To restore what had been taken or removed
To restore to a previous state
H8421H.detail:
1. To render means to give back to someone what belongs to them or what had been taken from them: it is to return into their hands. In Ezra 6:5, it refers to returning the gold and silver utensils of the temple that Nebuchadnezzar had taken to Babylon — restoring them to Jerusalem, to their rightful place.
2. To restore means to bring back what was missing: not only to give back, but to ensure that things return to their natural place. This is the sense of restoring a confiscated or stolen property.
3. To restore to a previous state: to return a place or an object to its original condition. The temple receives its precious adornments as it had before the exile; this is an act of restoration that marks the return to normalcy after disaster.
H8421H.origine: The Aramaic verb תּוּב (tuv) expresses the idea of return and restitution. It belongs to the family of words that speak of the movement of coming back, of turning around. The form used here (Aphel, a causative form) literally means "to make return" or "to cause to be restored" — that is, to implement the return of something to its master or to its place. This verb appears infrequently in the preserved Aramaic biblical texts.
H8421H.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew and Aramaic Bible, at the heart of the decree of Cyrus reported in Ezra (6:5). The context is that of the end of the Babylonian exile: after seventy years, God inspires the Persian king Cyrus to order the restoration of the temple in Jerusalem. The treasures that had been plundered during the destruction of the temple in 586 BC must be returned. This unique verb summarizes the hope of the people: restitution, the return to the old order, the end of deprivation. It is a word of restoration and grace.
H8421H.portee: This word embodies the biblical promise that God does not leave His people in exile forever. The restitution of the temple utensils is not a mere administrative act: it is a sign that worship can resume, that God welcomes His people again, and that the order created by Him is restored. For the believer, "to render" speaks of the restoration that only God can accomplish: He recovers what was lost, brings it home, and restores it.

sens: To give an answer, a reply to someone
To return, to send something back
To restore, to put back in order
H8421I.detail:
1. To respond means to give a verbal answer to a question or remark: it is the act of speaking in return. In Daniel 3:16, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego "responded" to the king, meaning they gave him a direct answer to his words. This is also the sense of "to address" in Daniel 2:14, when Daniel spoke to Arioch: he responded in a way to the situation by speaking to him.
2. To return or send back means to bring something back to its owner or to its starting point — to return it into the hands of the one who sent it. This is the idea of receiving a letter or a report: in Ezra 5:5, the sending of a report and the receiving of a letter describe an exchange where a written response is returned.
3. To restore or put back in order means to bring something back to its previous state, to repair or to reestablish — a nuance that extends the idea of "return."
H8421I.origine: The Aramaic root תּוּב (tuv) fundamentally means "to return" or "to come back." It is closely related to the Hebrew שׁוּב (shuv), which carries the same meaning and image: to turn around, to return to a starting point. The idea of "responding" naturally derives from this: to respond is to "return" the word to the one who spoke to you, to send back an answer as one would return an object.
H8421I.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears four times in the official texts of Ezra and Daniel in Aramaic. It mainly occurs in contexts of communication: responding to a king (Daniel 2:14 and 3:16), where it involves speaking in the face of authority; or in royal administration (Ezra 5:5 and 5:11), where it designates the sending of reports and the receiving of official letters. The word thus has both a social significance (direct, dialogical response) and an administrative one (circulation of documents).
H8421I.portee: This word reminds us that responding is an important act: it is to take the floor in front of someone, often in front of authority. In Daniel, the three young men "respond" to the king with wisdom and courage, showing that speech can be an act of faithfulness and trust in God, even in the face of human power. To respond is also to establish a relationship: one can only engage in dialogue if one returns the word to the other.

sens: Son of Japheth and grandson of Noah
Region of the Caucasus and Asia Minor
H8422G.detail:
1. Tubal is one of the seven sons of Japheth, himself a son of Noah. He appears in the genealogies of the early nations after the flood (Genesis 10:2 and 1 Chronicles 1:5), alongside his brothers Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Meshech, and Tiras. Like many names on this list, Tubal designates both an ancient person and the people or region that descended from him.
2. Tubal also becomes the name of a region in eastern Asia Minor, probably the land of the Tibareni, located in the Caucasus and Cappadocia. This distant land is associated in the Bible with warrior peoples and metallurgy.
H8422G.origine: The name Tubal literally means "you will be brought" or "you will be led" (from a root meaning "to bring, to carry"). It is a typical name in pre-flood genealogies, where names are often prophetic or descriptive statements. Tubal represents one of the twelve nations descended from Noah through his three sons (Shem, Ham, and Japheth), whose descendants repopulated the earth after the flood.
H8422G.emploi: Tubal appears only twice in the Bible, solely in genealogical lists: once in Genesis 10:2 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:5, in a nearly identical context. These two occurrences enumerate the sons of Japheth immediately after the flood. The biblical context first designates Tubal as a person (the patriarchal ancestor), and then by extension as the people and region he founded. This distant region is mentioned once in Ezekiel 27:13 and 32:26, but in a different form (Tubal) and as a commercial or warrior power of later times.

sens: Region of ancient Asia Minor, probably corresponding to Cappadocia
Trading people or nation mentioned alongside other peoples of the time
Future power enemy of Israel in eschatological prophecy
H8422H.detail:
1. Tubal refers to a historical region located in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), probably Cappadocia or a neighboring area. It appears as a distant land, beyond the borders of the world known to Israel (Isaiah 66:19).
2. It is a people or nation that engaged in trade and produced bronze utensils, exchanging its goods with other commercial powers of its time such as Tyre (Ezekiel 27:13).
3. In the prophecy of Ezekiel, Tubal appears as a territory and a people associated with Gog and other nations in a great eschatological coalition directed against Israel, thus designating a hostile power in the end times (Ezekiel 38:2-3; 39:1).
H8422H.origine: The name Tubal, like many names of biblical peoples and regions, is of geographical origin. According to tradition, this name evokes "that which must be brought" or "that which will be led," an allusion to its role as a distant region from which goods and peoples come. It is often mentioned alongside other territories of Asia Minor such as Meshech and Rosh, in contexts of trade or conflict.
H8422H.emploi: Tubal appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in prophecies. In Isaiah 66:19, it is listed among the distant nations to which God will send His witnesses to proclaim His glory. In Ezekiel 27:13, it is presented as an established trading partner, trafficking with Tyre and exporting slaves and bronze. However, the context completely changes in Ezekiel 38-39 (three occurrences), where Tubal becomes the territory of a hostile power: it is associated with Gog, an apocalyptic war leader, and forms with other nations a threat against Israel on the day of the Lord.
H8422H.portee: For the believing reader, Tubal serves as a reminder that God knows and rules not only over the nations close to Israel but also over distant and powerful nations. In the prophecies of Ezekiel, the mention of Tubal alongside Gog invites spiritual vigilance: the enemies of Israel, however formidable they may seem, will fall under God's judgment in the end times. This name thus reinforces the certainty that the Lord's sovereignty extends over all peoples and nations.

sens: region of ancient Asia Minor, probably in Cappadocia
H8422I.detail: 1. Tubal refers to a geographical region of the ancient Near East, located in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), probably equivalent to Cappadocia. In Ezekiel 32:26, it is mentioned alongside Meshech as a people that spread terror on the earth and lies dead by the sword, its graves surrounded by those who knew it.
H8422I.origine: The name Tubal, in its original etymology, would mean "you shall be brought" or "you shall be led," possibly referring to an action of transport or exodus. It is a historically well-attested region in ancient Asia Minor, often associated with the peoples of the northern and eastern Mediterranean.
H8422I.emploi: Tubal appears only once in the Bible in the Segond 1910, in Ezekiel 32:26. It is mentioned in a prophetic oracle against Egypt and its allies, listing the peoples and regions that have suffered death by the sword and lie in the realm of the dead. This mention places Tubal among the powers of the time that have disappeared from the world of the living, testifying to the extent of divine judgment.

sens: Son of Lamech and Zillah, brother of Jabal and Jubal
First man to be a blacksmith, inventor of metalworking techniques
Archetypal figure of technical progress and human skill
H8423.detail:
1. Tubal-Caïn is the son that Zillah bore to Lamech. He is the brother of Jabal, who was a shepherd, and Jubal, who invented music (Genesis 4:22). His three half-brothers (from Lamech's other wife, Ada) show how pre-flood humanity diversified into different trades and arts.
2. Tubal-Caïn "forged all kinds of tools of bronze and iron" (Genesis 4:22). He is presented as the first blacksmith in history, the one who discovered how to transform raw metals into useful tools and weapons. He is a man of skill and technical innovation.
3. Through his skill and inventiveness, Tubal-Caïn represents the creative genius of humanity, its ability to progress and dominate nature through technology. Along with his brothers Jabal and Jubal, he embodies how the descendants of Cain brought major innovations before the flood.
H8423.origine: The name means "you shall be brought (from) Cain" or relates to metalworking. Tubal-Caïn belongs to the lineage of Cain, the first murderer: he descends from Cain and Enoch, his son. His patronymic incorporates the name of his ancestor Cain, thus marking the continuity of this cursed lineage that continues to progress in power and technical ability before being wiped out by the flood.
H8423.emploi: Tubal-Caïn appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 4:22. He is mentioned in the pre-flood genealogy of Cain, alongside Jabal and Jubal, his brothers. The Bible specifically presents him as the first blacksmith, the one who mastered bronze and iron. This technical detail underscores that the lineage of Cain, although destined to be judged (since it will disappear in the flood), nevertheless contributed to the advancement of human arts and techniques. His existence shows that technical progress is an ancient and natural human capacity.
H8423.portee: Tubal-Caïn reminds us that talent, skill, and technical innovation are ancient gifts of humanity, but also that technological mastery does not save from divine condemnation: his lineage, despite its accomplishments, perished in the flood. His story invites the Christian to see human progress not as an absolute or a way of salvation, but as a created reality that God judges according to His sovereign justice.

sens: Deep pain, sadness that weighs on the soul
Moral affliction, pain of the heart
Cause of sadness or disappointment
H8424.detail:
1. Sorrow is a deep pain that weighs down the soul: the psalmist says, "My soul weeps from sorrow" (Psalms 119:28), expressing a sadness that overwhelms the heart and the entire body. It is an intense affliction, often accompanied by tears.
2. It is also the moral pain one feels in the face of disappointment or misfortune: the heart can be afflicted and shift from laughter to distress (Proverbs 14:13), for sorrow sometimes hides beneath appearances. It is an inner wound that persists.
3. In a causative sense, sorrow is what causes pain to someone: a foolish son becomes the sorrow of his mother (Proverbs 10:1), just as one who gives birth to a fool will have sorrow (Proverbs 17:21). Sorrow then designates the subject that provokes the suffering of others.
H8424.origine: The Hebrew word תּוּגָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of weight, oppression, that which weighs heavily. The image is that of a burden that overwhelms: sorrow is not a light emotion, but an affliction that presses on the heart. It is a word from the Wisdom literature of Israel, frequent in the Psalms and Proverbs to describe the states of the heart.
H8424.emploi: This word appears four times in the Bible, only in the Psalms and Proverbs, books that explore the inner states of the soul. In Proverbs, it mainly denotes the sorrow that a foolish child causes to his parents: it is a pain that the behavior of others provokes in us (Proverbs 10:1, 17:21). In Psalm 119, it is a personal pain that overwhelms the psalmist himself and affects him to the point of bending him (Psalms 119:28). The word thus oscillates between suffering endured and suffering caused, reflecting the two sides of human sorrow.
H8424.portee: Sorrow reminds us that life involves pain and disappointment, and that it is not without significance: our words and actions shape the hearts of those who love us. For the afflicted believer, acknowledging his sorrow is also about entrusting it to God and seeking His support. For those who weigh on others, it is an invitation to repent and change.

sens: Son of Gomer, grandson of Japheth, great-grandson of Noah
Territory or region inhabited by the descendants of Togarma
H8425G.detail:
1. Togarma is a man living in the time of the Patriarchs, listed among the sons of Gomer in the genealogies of Genesis 10. He is part of the family of Japheth, one of Noah's three sons. According to Genesis 10:3, he is the brother of Ashkenaz and Riphath, all three descendants of the people of the Gomerites.
2. Beyond the person, Togarma also designates a geographical region, probably in Armenia, which would have been occupied by the descendants of the patriarch. This territory bears the name of its eponymous ancestor, a common practice in the Old Testament where peoples and their lands receive the name of their founder.
H8425G.origine: The name Togarma means "you will break." Its etymology comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the action of breaking or shattering. Togarma appears only in the genealogical lists of Genesis 10 and 1 Chronicles 1, which trace the descendants of Noah after the Flood and the dispersion of peoples. It is a patriarchal name, given to an individual who then founded a people or a region bearing his name.
H8425G.emploi: Togarma appears only twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists. In Genesis 10:3, he is listed among the sons of Gomer, enumerated as ancestors of the peoples descended from Japheth. This passage constitutes the first mention of Togarma and establishes his place in the genealogical tree of humanity after the Flood. In 1 Chronicles 1:6, the same Togarma appears in a parallel repetition of these genealogies, confirming his foundational role of a people or region. These two references show that Togarma was a significant name for the genealogies of Israel, allowing for the positioning of neighboring peoples within the divine order of creation and post-diluvian dispersion.
H8425G.portee: Togarma reminds the reader that the Bible is not limited to the history of Israel: it places the people of God within a universal history where every people, every nation, descends from Noah and has its place in God's plans. These genealogies establish that distant nations are not foreign to the divine purpose, but are part of it, whether they know it or not. For the Christian, this perspective invites seeing all peoples as creations of God deserving of the Gospel.

sens: Region or people from the north of Asia Minor, probably ancient Armenia
Descendants of Togarmah, son of Gomer
Suppliers of horses and horsemen
Allies from the north against Israel in prophetic visions
H8425H.detail: 1. Togarma designates a region inhabited by the descendants of Togarmah. It likely corresponds to ancient Armenia and the neighboring territories of the Caucasus, in the north of Asia Minor. 2. It is a trading people: in Ezekiel 27:14, the "house of Togarma" provides horses, horsemen, and mules to Tyre, showing its importance in ancient Near Eastern trade. 3. In the prophetic vision of Ezekiel 38:6, Togarma represents a military power from the north that allies with Gog and his troops against Israel, symbolizing the distant and formidable enemy forces that threaten the people of God in the last days.
H8425H.origine: Togarmah is the name of a son of Gomer (himself a son of Japheth, son of Noah) according to the Table of Nations in Genesis 10. The name means "you will break." The region named after his descendants extends into the north of the known world of antiquity, an area of significant military and commercial power.
H8425H.emploi: Togarma appears twice in the book of Ezekiel, in two different contexts. First in 27:14, in the prophetic lament over the fall of Tyre, where it is listed among the peoples that trade with the great Phoenician city, particularly known for exporting horses and horsemen. Then in 38:6, in the apocalyptic vision of the end times, where it is mentioned as one of the northern nations that will join Gog in a final attack against Israel. These two usages show that Togarma was known as a distant power, militarily strong and strategically significant.
H8425H.portee: Togarma reminds the biblical reader that God knows and controls all the peoples of the earth, even those that seem distant and powerful. Its mention alongside Gog in the vision of the last days assures the people of God that, no matter how threatening hostile coalitions may appear, the final victory belongs to the Lord.

sens: Sacrificial offering brought to God in acknowledgment of a blessing received
Praise and acknowledgment expressed through song or word in worship
Procession or group of people proclaiming gratitude to God
Public confession made before God and the people
H8426.detail: 1. Thanksgiving is primarily a sacrifice offered to God to thank Him for a grace received: in Leviticus 7:12, this sacrifice is brought with cakes and unleavened bread, as a material offering that accompanies heartfelt gratitude. 2. It is also the praise itself, the song or word by which we thank God; in Psalms 100:4, we enter God's courts with praise and songs, meaning we express our gratitude vocally. 3. The word also designates a procession or a group of people who collectively proclaim their gratitude; in Nehemiah 12:38, a choir marches on the wall of Jerusalem to celebrate the reconstruction of the temple. 4. Finally, thanksgiving can be a public confession or acknowledgment: in Joshua 7:19, someone is asked to make known to God by confessing the wrong they have committed, which shows that acknowledgment also involves admitting the truth before God.
H8426.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to give account, confess, praise." The initial image is that of acknowledgment or declaration: we recognize God's goodness by praising Him, just as we acknowledge a fault by confessing it. This same Hebrew word appears in other forms to designate one who praises or confesses. Thanksgiving encompasses the idea that recognizing God's blessings means publicly acknowledging them, bearing witness to them.
H8426.emploi: The word appears about 30 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms and historical books. It is very common in worship contexts: the Psalms use it to designate the praise directed to God in the temple (Psalms 50:23, 100:4). In the Law, it corresponds to a specific type of sacrifice offered in fulfillment of a vow or in thanksgiving (Leviticus 7:12). At the time of the return from exile, the word also takes on the meaning of solemn procession, as in Nehemiah 12:38 where groups of Levites form choirs of thanksgiving that traverse the wall of Jerusalem. The meaning can extend to public confession, as in Joshua 7:19. Everywhere, the word implies that recognizing God should not be done in silence, but through an audible and often collective declaration.
H8426.portee: Thanksgiving teaches us that gratitude towards God should not remain buried in the heart, but should be expressed openly, through song, word, or even gesture. It invites us to transform our blessings into public praise, and to openly confess, in the temple or elsewhere, what God has done for us. It is a way to glorify God and to testify to others that we have recognized Him as the source of all good.

sens: Make a visible trace or sign on something
Inscribe or imprint a mark as a seal or sign of recognition
Designate someone by a distinctive sign
H8427.detail:
1. Make a visible trace or sign on something: this is creating a physical mark, often in a repeated or frantic manner. David, in 1 Samuel 21:13, made marks on the doorposts while behaving like a madman — it was a chaotic gesture, without a specific purpose, to give the impression that he was out of his mind.
2. Inscribe or imprint a mark as a seal or sign of recognition: this is leaving a trace that identifies or protects. In Ezekiel 9:4, the angel marks the foreheads of the righteous — not to confuse, but to distinguish and protect them during the judgment that will fall upon the city.
3. Designate someone by a distinctive sign: this is using a mark to show to whom a person belongs or to identify them in the crowd of others. The mark then becomes a seal of covenant, possession, or divine protection.
H8427.origine: The Hebrew verb tavah expresses the action of tracing, engraving, or limiting by a mark. Its basic image is that of a hand tracing a line or a visible sign. This word is infrequent in biblical Hebrew, which makes its appearance all the more significant: it emphasizes the concrete act of marking, leaving a lasting imprint.
H8427.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, which shows that the vocabulary of marking was generally expressed by other words. In both cases, it involves leaving a visible trace. In 1 Samuel 21:13, David marks the doors in a disorderly manner, like a madman. In Ezekiel 9:4, the meaning is radically different: the mark becomes an act of salvation, a divine sign that separates the righteous from the wicked. The context transforms the simple act of tracing into a gesture loaded with theological meaning.
H8427.portee: To mark is to distinguish, protect, identify. For the believer, this image reminds us that God knows His own and marks them with His sign. It also evokes the promise of protection: those whom God marks are safe from judgment. It is a comforting image of the relationship between God and His people.

sens: Cause pain, suffering to someone
Irritate, offend by repeated provocation
Test divine patience
H8428.detail:
1. The word describes the action of causing moral or spiritual suffering to someone, particularly through acts or words that hurt. It is a strong word, evoking less simple annoyance than an intentionally inflicted wound.
2. It takes on the meaning of irritating or offending someone by constantly challenging them. In Psalms 78:41, Israel "provokes" the holy God by continually testing Him with their murmurs and unbelief, as if the people were trying to make Him react through a succession of rebellions.
3. The word expresses the idea of tempting God, that is, pushing Him to the limit, challenging Him by doubting His word and power, despite all the signs He has given.
H8428.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of causing pain or injury. It is related to verbs expressing suffering and affliction. The form used here (Hiphil) is one that causes or provokes the action: it carries the idea of inflicting pain on others.
H8428.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 78:41. It is found in a historical and liturgical context: the psalmist recounts how Israel continually tempted and provoked the Lord in the wilderness, despite the wonders He performed. The verb "provoke" captures the repeated and deliberate nature of the people's rebellion — it is not an isolated deviation, but a continuous attitude of defiance towards God.
H8428.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the seriousness of repeated unbelief and doubt towards God. It shows that constantly contesting God is to hurt Him, provoke Him, and test Him in an offensive manner. For the believer, it serves as a warning against the habit of murmuring and doubting, even after witnessing God's faithfulness.

sens: Experience sudden and intense fear
Be seized with a fright that disturbs the mind and prompts hasty action
H8429.detail:
1. Experience sudden and intense fear: the word describes the moment when terror seizes someone in the face of an unexpected and alarming situation. It is a fright that arises abruptly, shaking the soul. King Nebuchadnezzar in the midst of events "was afraid" upon realizing that four men, not three, were walking in the flames (Daniel 3:24).
2. Be seized with a fright that disturbs the mind and prompts hasty action: this fear is not passive; it provokes an immediate reaction. Nebuchadnezzar, frightened, "rose up quickly" — his terror set him in motion, prompting him to react without delay.
H8429.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root expressing the idea of being troubled, disturbed, thrown into disorder by sudden fear. It is a state verb that describes less a voluntary action than an involuntary seizing of the heart and mind in the face of the unexpected and the abnormal.
H8429.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 3:24, at the climax of the story of the three young men in the furnace. The context is that of a supernatural event: Nebuchadnezzar sees a fourth person in the flames, which terrifies him and leads him to question his advisors. The king's fear marks a turning point in the narrative, as he will recognize the presence and power of the God of Israel.
H8429.portee: This fear of the king in the face of God's supernatural work reminds us that God's miracles produce terror in those who witness them. It also shows how fear can open the heart to the recognition of God and humility before His sovereignty.

sens: Levite from the time of the united monarchy, ancestor of the prophet Samuel
H8430.detail: 1. Toah is a man from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time when the twelve tribes of Israel were under a single king. He appears in the genealogy of the prophet Samuel: in 1 Chronicles 6:34, he is presented as the son of Elkana and the father of Eliel. This name designates a key generation in the lineage of those who will serve God at the sanctuary.
H8430.origine: The name Toah means "humble" or "lowly" in Hebrew. It is a unique name that appears only once in the Bible, designating this specific Levite. In the Hebrew text, it is also encountered in the form Tohu (H8459 תֹּחוּ), indicating that it is a variant of the same name.
H8430.emploi: Toah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:34. He is included in the long genealogy of the Levites who served at the sanctuary, particularly in the lineage descending from Levi himself. His importance arises from the fact that he is the ancestor of the prophet Samuel, one of the greatest men of God in the Old Testament. This genealogy shows that Samuel was not an unknown figure, but came from a family of Levites dedicated to divine service.
H8430.portee: For the reader, Toah reminds us that even men whose names are known only — who are never seen acting or speaking in biblical narratives — play their role in God's plan. His place in Samuel's genealogy shows us that God uses entire generations, ordinary ancestors, to prepare His most important servants. This encourages the believer to understand that their faithfulness, even humble and discreet, is part of a larger divine project.

sens: confident expectation of a better future
what one hopes to obtain or see realized
feeling of confidence directed towards the future
the object or person in whom one places their hope
H8431.detail:
1. Hope is a forward-looking expectation, mixed with confidence. It is not a mere passive curiosity, but a heart orientation that awaits something good. In Job 40:28, one who places their hope in their own strength is mistaken: they are counting on something that will not hold.
2. It is also what one concretely expects — the good that one hopes to receive. In Proverbs 10:28, the "expectation" of the righteous is the reward and happiness that God prepares for them.
3. Hope can refer to the inner feeling itself, that movement of the heart that refuses to despair. In Proverbs 13:12, "a deferred hope makes the heart sick": waiting long without results wears down the heart.
4. Finally, it can personify the person or reality in whom one hopes. In Psalms 39:8, "my hope" means "the one in whom I hope" — the Lord Himself. In Lamentations 3:18, losing hope in the Lord means losing the one who sustains life.
H8431.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to wait," "to stretch towards." It literally designates the thread that is stretched, then the action of waiting while stretching towards.
