This image of tension, of heart direction, explains why hope is always active: it is an expectation that does not give up, pulling the soul forward. The root is found in several words of the same family meaning "cord," "tie" — what connects the one who hopes to what they hope for.
H8431.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Job, Psalms) and in Lamentations. It always designates an expectation directed towards a future good. In Proverbs, the hope of the righteous is regularly contrasted with that of the wicked: one endures and bears fruit (Proverbs 10:28), the other will perish (Proverbs 11:7). Hope can also be directed towards a person — the Psalmist says to God, "you are my hope" (Psalms 39:8) — which shows that true rest of the heart consists in fixing one's expectation on the One who is reliable. The word can finally express how the absence of hope gnaws at the soul: in Lamentations 3:18, the prophet plunges into despair when he stops expecting from the Lord.
H8431.portee: This biblical hope is not a vague optimism, but a heart orientation directed towards the good that one knows God can give. It implies refusing to despair, even under suffering or waiting. The Bible reveals that true hope rests on a person — the faithful God — rather than on circumstances or our own strength. That is why the righteous can maintain hope when everything collapses around them: their expectation is not fixed on the changing world, but on the One who remains.

sens: Central point or central area of a space, object, or zone
Space or area through which one passes, by which one crosses
Group of people within which someone or something is found
Space separating two things arranged face to face
Source or origin: drawn from within a group or situation
H8432.detail:
1. The "midst" is the point or central area of a space: the tree of life was planted in the midst of the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:9), meaning at the heart of that place. It is the spot where several directions converge, the geographical center of a region or object.
2. This word also designates the space through which one crosses, the path or passage through something: when the Israelites walked in the midst of the Red Sea, they advanced through its waters (Exodus 14:22).
3. The "midst" can mean "among," inside a group of people: the Lord tells Jeroboam that He raised him from the midst of the people, meaning He chose him from among the Israelites (1 Kings 14:7). It indicates someone or something within a community.
4. Between two objects or two people arranged face to face, the midst indicates the space that separates them: this is the sense of "between" (Genesis 15:10, where Abraham divides the animals in two parts).
5. Finally, "from the midst of" indicates origin or provenance: coming out from the midst of a crowd means being extracted from it or removed from it (Jeremiah 37:12; 1 Kings 14:7).
H8432.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "division" or "sharing" — the midst is what divides a whole into two halves. The primary notion is spatial and geometric: the center that divides equally. In Aramaic, a similar form is found. The word is already used in the earliest biblical texts with this same meaning: physical at first, then extended figuratively to express "among" or "within."
H8432.emploi: This word appears about 390 times in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the Pentateuch and historical books. It is first used in a precise spatial sense: the midst of the garden, of the Jordan, of the camp. Very quickly, it acquires a relational sense: "among" a people or assembly. In the laws of Leviticus and Numbers, "in the midst" means "in the presence of" or "among you" (Leviticus 15:31). The context of motion (crossing, coming out) enriches its meaning: after a verb of movement, it expresses passage through (Exodus 14:22, Exodus 14:27). In the prophets, this word retains its symbolic charge: God dwells "in the midst" of His people (Exodus 29:45) as a sign of His presence and covenant.
H8432.portee: This word reminds us that God places good (the tree of life) at the center of human life and that He dwells in the midst of His people. It expresses the intimacy of the relationship with God, not as a distant force but as a central presence. For the Christian, this invites recognition that God is not on the margins of existence: He is in its heart, at the heart of the Church. This word also helps to understand the biblical notion of separation and choice: being drawn from the midst means being set apart for a mission.

sens: Penalty, sanction imposed to correct a fault
Reprimand, reproach that corrects one who goes astray
Painful trial sent by God to correct His people
H8433A.detail:
1. Punishment is the penalty one receives for wrongdoing. It is an unfortunate, often painful consequence, intended to rectify the fault. In 2 Kings 19:3, Hezekiah speaks of a "day of distress, punishment, and reproach" — he refers to the critical moment when God sanctions the people for their sins.
2. Punishment can also be a verbal correction, a reprimand aimed at redirecting one who goes astray. This is expressed in Psalm 149:7 when it asks God "to execute vengeance on the nations, to punish the peoples" — a divine intervention that corrects and brings back to order.
3. More broadly, it is the trial itself that God sends — an illness, a military defeat, a disaster — to sanction evil and bring His people to repentance. In Hosea 5:9, "Ephraim will be devastated on the day of punishment" refers to the ruin of the kingdom as a consequence of divine judgment.
H8433A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to push away" or "to straighten." It is linked to the idea of active correction: the one who receives punishment is put back on the right path, like straightening a bent branch. The same root gives rise to other words in the family of correction and judgment.
H8433A.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of crisis or divine judgment. It designates either a moment of national affliction (2 Kings 19:3 and Isaiah 37:3 — the same passage in duplicate — which speak of the siege of Jerusalem), or the divine action of punishment exercised on a people or nation (Psalms 149:7, Hosea 5:9). In all cases, punishment is never arbitrary: it responds to guilt and aims at correction, not gratuitous destruction.
H8433A.portee: For the believer reading these texts, punishment reminds us that God takes justice seriously and that evil acts have consequences. But this word also shows that divine judgment is not blind: it is a form of correction, an invitation to return to God. Understanding this helps to read calamities not as absurd curses, but as calls to repentance and return.

sens: word that reproaches and corrects
punishment, penalty inflicted to correct
argument presented to defend or convince
warning or correction intended to instruct
H8433B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a strong word that reproaches someone for their fault or error, with the intention of correcting them. It is the act of telling someone: "You have acted wrongly." We see this in Proverbs 12:1, where he who loves correction loves knowledge, while he who hates reprimand is foolish.
2. It can also mean the punishment itself, the physical or moral chastisement that sanctions a fault. Proverbs 3:11 invites the son not to despise the Lord's correction and not to be frightened by His chastisements: these are the blows or trials through which God corrects.
3. The word can finally designate an argument put forward to defend oneself or refute an opponent — a word that opposes another to establish the truth. In Job 13:6, Job asks to be listened to: he wants to present his defense and for his lips to state their reply before those who accuse him.
4. Overall, it is a warning or lesson given to instruct and advance: hence why Proverbs 15:31 says that the attentive ear to reprimands that lead to life dwells among the wise.
H8433B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to reproach, to contest." It expresses the idea of opposing someone, contradicting their conduct or words. It is a term from judicial and educational language: the one who reprimands exposes the error or guilt so that the offender may correct themselves. The root also appears in other forms used to express argument, complaint, or accusation.
H8433B.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Proverbs, but also in Psalms, Job, Ezekiel, and Habakkuk. In Proverbs, it almost always characterizes educational correction: that which a wise person gives to a child or a fool to lead them to wisdom. In Job, it takes on a more judicial meaning: Job wants to present his defense against his accusers. In the Psalms (38:15, 39:12), it is often the punishment that the psalmist fears or suffers from God. In the prophets (Ezekiel), it sometimes becomes a calamity inflicted on nations as divine judgment, a sign that other peoples will recognize God's justice.
H8433B.portee: This word reminds the believer that a reprimand is not simply anger, but a pathway to wisdom and righteous living. Receiving correction with humility rather than rejecting it is the way to spiritual growth. It also shows that God does not abandon those He loves: discipline is a mark of affection, not vengeance. For the teacher or leader, this word invites to correct straightforwardly, knowing that truth spoken firmly can save.

sens: city in the territory of Simeon
H8434.detail: Tholad is a small city that belonged to the territory of the tribe of Simeon in ancient Israel. It is mentioned in the enumeration of Simeon's localities in 1 Chronicles 4:29, alongside Bilhah and Etsem, which helps us locate it in this region of southern Israel.
H8434.origine: The name Tholad literally means "generation" in Hebrew (from the root "tolad"), but it designates a specific place here. The name may have been given to this place due to a tradition or a forgotten founding event. The word is also known in the form "El-tolad" in ancient texts.
H8434.emploi: Tholad appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:29, in the list of cities in the territory of Simeon. This enumeration helps to delineate the territory tributary during the days of the Israelite monarchy. No particular event is reported about Tholad; it simply appears among the cities of this district of Simeon.

sens: descendants of a person or family
genealogical enumeration of these descendants
history or succession of events of a family or people
set of what is born or arises from
H8435.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the children and direct descendants of a person. This is seen when we say "the posterity of Jacob" (Genesis 37:2) or "the posterity of Terach," meaning his sons, Abram, Nahor, and Haran (Genesis 11:27).
2. It can also describe a complete genealogical list, an ordered enumeration of successive generations that recounts who begot whom. Thus Genesis 5:1 begins with "This is the book of the generations of Adam," which introduces the entire chain of descendants.
3. The word also applies to the systematic classification of a group: in Numbers 1:24, they "register the sons of Gad according to their families," meaning they are ordered and counted according to their lineage.
4. More broadly, it can mean the history of a people or the order of things according to which they are born: Genesis 2:4 speaks of the "origins of the heavens and the earth" at the time of their creation, the sequence of cosmic events.
H8435.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to give birth, to beget." It belongs to the family of words that speak of birth and lineage. The plural (toledoth) is often used at the beginning of important sections of Genesis to signify not only a descent but the complete account of what arises from it. It is a term that links together the idea of family generation and that of historical continuity.
H8435.emploi: This word appears 39 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis, Exodus, and Chronicles. Genesis uses it as a hinge to mark the major milestones of the creation narrative and the patriarchal families: "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 2:4), or the generations of Adam (5:1), Noah (10:1), Abraham (25:12). In Numbers, it serves to organize the counting of the people according to tribes and families (Numbers 1:20-42): each group is enumerated "according to their families." In Chronicles, it is used for genealogical lists establishing the order of ancestors and descendants. The word thus oscillates between the concrete meaning of "family lineage" and the more abstract meaning of "historical succession" or "order of generations."
H8435.portee: This word reminds us that in biblical history, generations are intertwined: God does not deal with individuals in isolation, but in the continuity of their families and peoples. It is a call to recognize our place in the chain of past and future generations, and to understand that our lives are part of a design that transcends us. For the believer, this invites us to see how God guides history through human families.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Old Testament
H8436.detail: Thilon is a man of the tribe of Judah, son of Shimon. He appears in the genealogy of the sons of Judah listed in 1 Chronicles 4:20, alongside his brothers Amnon, Rinnah, and Ben-Hanan. This is the only mention of this character in the Bible.
H8436.origine: The name Thilon literally means "gift" or "present" in Hebrew, reflecting a common practice among ancient Hebrews to give meaningful names to their children. This name expresses the idea that the child is a gift from God to their parents.
H8436.emploi: Thilon is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:20, where he appears in the genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. This genealogy, although brief, shows the importance that biblical writers placed on the transmission of tribal and family lineages, even for minor characters whose stories are not told elsewhere.

sens: One who torments and burdens a people, who subjugates them by force
H8437.detail: 1. The oppressor is a person or group that subjugates others through violence and deprives them of freedom. The word evokes a weight, an overwhelming domination. In Psalm 137, it refers to the Babylonians who conquered Jerusalem and took the Jews into exile: these "oppressors" demanded that the captives sing, which shows the cruelty of those who humiliate their prisoners.
H8437.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means torment and oppression. It belongs to a family of words related to the idea of conflict, domination, and suffering inflicted on a weak or defeated people.
H8437.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 137:3, where it specifically refers to the Babylonian oppressors who destroyed Jerusalem and deported the people of Judah. The context of the psalm is that of exile, and the term reflects the bitterness of the captive people in the face of their conquerors.
H8437.portee: For the Christian who suffers or sees others suffering injustice and oppression, this word reminds that God sees the cruelty of the powerful. The psalms of exile express a confidence that God will not allow oppressors to triumph forever and that divine justice will be fulfilled.

sens: Parasitic worm whose dried body produces a dye
Crimson dye obtained from this worm
Fabric dyed this purple color
Figuratively: wealth, luxury, and honor
H8438A.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the female worm from which a precious red dye was once extracted. This tiny worm, which lives on certain oaks, has been sought since antiquity for the quality of its dye.
2. By extension, it names the dye itself, this crimson powder obtained by drying and grinding the body of the insect: it is this dye that Isaiah 1:18 speaks of when comparing sins to a scarlet hue that fades under divine forgiveness.
3. The word also refers to the fabrics or textiles dyed this magnificent color. Exodus 25:4 lists the materials for the Lord's tent: they sought "blue, purple, and scarlet yarns," as only the finest fabrics were suitable for the sanctuary.
4. Purple was so expensive and rare that it symbolized royalty, power, and wealth: this is why Lamentations 4:5 mentions those "who were raised in purple" to refer to the children of the rich and powerful now reduced to misery.
H8438A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the worm itself, this color-producing insect. The name of the worm thus gave its name to the hue and the fabrics dyed with it. This purple dye was known throughout the ancient Near East as the most prestigious and costly dye, reserved for kings and priests.
H8438A.emploi: The word appears about 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly to describe worship materials and signs of wealth. In Exodus 25:4, it is among the precious fabrics intended for the construction of the tent of meeting. In Isaiah 1:18, the text uses scarlet as an image of deeply rooted sin, since this hue was nearly indelible. In Lamentations 4:5, purple evokes the lost luxury of Jerusalem's nobles, who fell due to the city's destruction.
H8438A.portee: This word reminds the believer that true purity comes from God, not from wealth or prestige. When Isaiah declares that even sins as red as purple will be made white, he speaks of the transformative power of divine forgiveness, stronger than the most indelible dyes. Purple teaches us that God can renew one who seems irreparably marked.

sens: Small invertebrate animal, worm or larva, that feeds on organic matter
Insect that produces red dye (the kermes)
Red color obtained from this insect, used to dye fabrics
Symbol of decomposition, degradation, or mortality
H8438B.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a worm or larva, a tiny creature that crawls and feeds on what decays: "I am a worm, and not a man," says the Psalmist expressing his humiliation (Psalm 22:7). 2. It specifically refers to the insect called kermes (coccus ilicis), from which a precious red dye was extracted. 3. This dye was used to dye the fabrics of the tabernacle in crimson, including the curtains, veils, priestly garments, and embroideries (Exodus 26:1, 28:8, 39:1, 39:29). 4. Finally, the worm symbolizes human weakness, insignificance, and the mortal destiny of man: "You will no longer be a numerous people; your dead are countless, the worms will cover them" (Isaiah 14:11), or the eternal dwelling of the reprobate where "the worm does not die" (Isaiah 66:24).
H8438B.origine: The Hebrew word תּוֹלֵעָה comes from a root expressing the idea of worm or larva. The insect it refers to, the kermes, has been known since antiquity for its ability to produce an intense red dye; hence the French word "crimson." The same root produces other Hebrew words designating worms or parasitic larvae. This dual nature—repugnant animal and source of precious color—reflects a characteristic tension of biblical symbols.
H8438B.emploi: The word appears 38 times in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus and related passages (26 occurrences), it almost exclusively refers to the crimson color used for the fabrics of the tabernacle: veils, carpets, belts, ephods, priestly garments (Exodus 26:1, 28:8, 35:35, 39:1, 39:29). In Leviticus 14, it appears three times in connection with the purification rite for the leper, where a piece of wool dyed crimson is used (Leviticus 14:4, 14:6, 14:49, 14:51, 14:52). In poetic and prophetic passages (Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Jonah), the word returns to its literal meaning of "worm" to express humiliation, mortality, and contempt: "I am a worm, and not a man" (Psalm 22:7), "your worms will not die" (Isaiah 66:24).
H8438B.portee: This word unites two opposing realities: the most despised creature, the worm that feeds on decay, and the most noble color, crimson that adorns the tabernacle and its servants. It reminds us that the beauty and holiness of worship paradoxically rest on what is abject; it also teaches us our own insignificance before God and the reality of death. Finally, the worm that accompanies the leper in his purification ritual symbolizes that the judgment of sin passes through the recognition of our humiliation.

sens: Son of Issachar, founder of the family of the Tolaites
Military leader and judge of Israel after Abimelech
H8439G.detail: Thola is one of the twelve sons of Issachar, named first in the genealogical lists (Genesis 46:13; 1 Chronicles 7:1). He gives his name to the family of the Tolaites, whose members are listed during the census in the wilderness (Numbers 26:23). His six sons—Uzzi, Rephaja, Jeriel, Jachmaï, Jibsam, and Samuel—are presented as valiant military leaders and numerous during the time of King David (1 Chronicles 7:2).
H8439G.origine: The name Thola means "worm" in Hebrew, possibly a familiar designation or related to an image of smallness. It is a personal name borne during the time of the patriarchs and in the wilderness.
H8439G.emploi: Thola appears in the Old Testament as a man from the tribe of Issachar living during the time of Egypt and the wilderness. He is first mentioned among the sons of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:13). His descendants, the Tolaites, form one of the families of Issachar (Numbers 26:23). His sons are listed as important and numerous warriors during the time of King David (1 Chronicles 7:1-2).

sens: Man of Israel, son of Puah, judge of the people after Abimelech
Eldest son of the tribe of Issachar and ancestor of the family of the Tholahites
H8439H.detail:
1. Thola is a man from the tribe of Issachar who, after the death of the tyrant Abimelech, rises up to deliver Israel from its oppressors by serving as a judge. He lives in Shamir, in the mountains of Ephraim, and represents a figure of salvation for the people at a time when they are in need (Judges 10:1).
2. Thola is also recognized as the eldest son of Issachar, one of the twelve tribes of Israel, and he is the founding ancestor of the family of the Tholahites, which bears his name and descends from him.
H8439H.origine: The name Thola literally means "worm" or "crimson" in Hebrew, an image that perhaps evokes smallness or humility. This name was borne in the tribe of Issachar, one of the twelve tribes born from the sons of Jacob, and it gave rise to the collective patronymic "Tholahites" to designate the descendants who claimed him.
H8439H.emploi: Thola appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 10:1, where he is presented as the son of Puah and the grandson of Dodo. After the death of Abimelech, who had oppressed Israel, Thola rises to judge the people and deliver them. Although the Bible does not provide details about his military exploits or specific actions as a judge, his mention indicates that he played an important role in restoring order and justice in Israel during the period of the judges.

sens: descendants of Tola, son of Issachar
H8440.detail: The Tholahites are the descendants of Tola, who was a son of the patriarch Issachar. During the census of the people of Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 26:23), the Tholahites are counted as one of the families of the clan of Issachar, which shows that this lineage formed a distinct and identifiable group within the tribe.
H8440.origine: The word comes from the name Tola (which means "worm" or "crimson" in Hebrew): Tola was the name of the son of Issachar from whom his descendants are derived. The suffix -ites or -aïtes in French indicates belonging to a descent or family group, following the common usage for naming family clans in Israel (like the Benjaminites for the descendants of Benjamin).
H8440.emploi: This term appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:23, during the second census of Israel in the wilderness. It designates one of the counting families in the tribe of Issachar, alongside the Puvites and the other families of Issachar. This census served to prepare for entry into the Promised Land by recording the numbers of each tribal descent.

sens: That which provokes disgust or horror
That which is forbidden by the Law, particularly in dietary or religious practices
That which is morally repugnant, contrary to justice and righteousness
That which is a serious violation of the heart or fidelity towards God
H8441.detail:
1. The word primarily designates something physically repugnant, that causes one to retch. In Genesis 43:32, the Egyptians find it "abominable" to eat with the Hebrews — it is a cultural and ritual repulsion, like that of a people facing food they deem impure or repulsive.

2. In the Law of Moses (Leviticus and Deuteronomy), the word applies to "unclean" things: certain animals, disordered sexual relations, statues of foreign gods. Deuteronomy 14:3 commands, "You shall not eat any abominable thing," and Deuteronomy 7:25-26 forbids desiring the "silver or gold" of idols, for "it is an abomination."

3. The word also takes on a moral and ethical sense: it designates unjust or dishonest acts. Proverbs 11:1 teaches that "false weights are an abomination to the Lord," just as Proverbs 12:22 states: lying is abominable in His eyes.

4. Ultimately, what wounds the heart of God Himself is an abomination: Ezekiel 6:9 speaks of idols whose "eyes have committed harlotry," and the nation takes "disgust because of its abominations." It is the refusal of fidelity to God that provokes His anger.
H8441.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root (tou'ab) that expresses repugnance, disgust. It is related to the idea of "recoiling from" or "having horror of." The Hebrew word appears mainly in the legislative books (Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in the prophets, particularly Ezekiel, who constantly enumerates the "abominations" of Israel and the nations. The corresponding Greek word in the Greek Old Testament (bdélugma, bdélussô) carries the same sense of ritual and moral disgust.
H8441.emploi: The word appears 112 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of the Law (Deuteronomy), in Kings and Chronicles (when kings introduce idol worship), and very frequently in Ezekiel and Proverbs. In Leviticus 18 and 20, it qualifies sexual acts contrary to the Law. In Deuteronomy, it also designates the practices of the Canaanite peoples: divination, witchcraft, child sacrifice (18:9-12). In Kings, whenever a king "does what is evil in the sight of the Lord," he "commits abominations" — idolatry, sacred prostitution (1 Kings 14:24, 2 Kings 21:2). Ezekiel makes it a dominant theme: Jerusalem has committed "abominations" that have led to captivity. Proverbs uses it for moral vices: a lying tongue, false weights, a haughty heart are all "abominable" to God. The meaning thus shifts from ritual (what defiles legal purity) to ethics (what defiles the soul).
H8441.portee: This word reminds us that God is not indifferent to evil: there is a divine disgust towards what violates His Law and character. For a believer, this invites us to hate what God hates — not only the great visible sins (idolatry, murder), but also the small dishonesties: lying, injustice, commercial dishonesty. The word also teaches that evil is not morally neutral: it is a horror, a deep violation that distances us from God. Recognizing our sins as "abominable" in His eyes can lead to repentance.

sens: Harm, material or moral damage
Impious, action contrary to the law of God
Confusion, disturbance
H8442.detail: 1. Damage is a harm or injury inflicted on someone, an attack on their property or reputation. It is the idea of evil that befalls a person, the blow that strikes them: in Jerusalem, enemies conspire to "cause damage" to the city, as one would bring down a wall (Nehemiah 4:8). 2. Damage can also refer to impiety, moral or religious perversity: the fool "commits impiety" (literally, the impious word becomes action), by speaking falsely and seeking to leave the soul of the hungry empty, that is, to leave them destitute (Isaiah 32:6). 3. More broadly, it is a confusion or disturbance of the just order: when someone "leaves empty" the rights of others, they sow disorder and wound the justice that God has established.
H8442.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of straying, deviating from the right path. It is related to the notions of moral error and religious deviation. The basic image is that of one who strays from the law or divine justice, who wanders far from the path laid out by God.
H8442.emploi: This word appears twice in the Old Testament, at both ends of the biblical testimony: first during the period of the reconstruction of the Temple (Nehemiah 4:8), where it designates the damage that enemies want to inflict on the walls of Jerusalem; then in the prophetic context of Isaiah (32:6), where it qualifies the impiety of one who takes advantage of the poor. The context determines the nuance: the word extends from physical damage to moral fault.
H8442.portee: This word reminds us that damage is not just a material accident, but often the work of one who rejects God. For the believer, it invites us to see the link between moral impiety and the evils that result: one who "commits impiety" by exploiting the poor chooses to inflict damage on their soul and that of others. It is a call to justice and the fear of the Lord.

sens: The highest point of a mountain or elevation
The dominant and imposing strength or power, like that of a lifted horn
The precious riches or resources that rise above all
H8443.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the peak of a mountain or height: the summit where majesty reigns (Psalms 95:4: "the peaks of the mountains").
2. The word also refers to the dominant, majestic power, that which stands tall — notably the virile strength of the buffalo with its lifted horns, an image of God's irresistible strength (Numbers 23:22: "the strength of the buffalo").
3. By extension, it evokes precious and dominant riches, that which rises and shines: gold, silver, the goods that crown life (Job 22:25: "the Almighty will be your gold, your silver, your wealth").
H8443.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of elevation and majesty, hence the image of the summit that dominates the landscape. The word is related to the idea of that which stands tall and impresses by its height. It is a poetic term that transports the physical image of the summit to realities of power, domination, and incomparable value.
H8443.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetry. In Numbers 23:22 and 24:8, it describes the strength of the buffalo — the virile and irresistible force — to express the divine power that liberated Israel from Egypt. In Job 22:25, it signifies the riches that constitute the true fortune of the faithful. In Psalms 95:4, it refers to the physical summit of the mountains, a symbol of God's sovereignty over all creation. The word thus plays on the ambiguity between physical height and spiritual or material dominance.
H8443.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that all that rises — power, wealth, majesty — belongs to God and emanates from Him. For the believer, it is a call to seek true strength and true riches in God, far beyond what the world can offer. Meditating on the summits of the mountains becomes a lesson on divine transcendence.

sens: extreme point where a line or boundary ends
place from which something comes or springs
exit or escape in the face of danger
H8444.detail:
1. The word designates the extremity or terminal point of a boundary: it is where a demarcation line ends and stops. When the tribes of Israel receive their territories, the Bible constantly describes how each boundary "ends" at the sea, the Jordan, or a mountain — it is the precise place where the limit concludes (Numbers 34:12: "it shall descend further to the Jordan, to end at the Salt Sea").
2. The word can also refer to the source or origin from which something springs — the opposite of the extremity in a sense of movement: that by which something begins or comes out. Proverbs 4:23 speaks of "keeping your heart" as the source of life, for it is from there that "the springs of life flow."
3. Finally, it can mean the outcome or escape, the possibility of getting away from death or danger — an emergency exit in a desperate situation.
H8444.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to go out" or "to go outside." The basic idea is thus a movement outward, toward the end or the exit. This is why it can designate both an extremity (where something ends up escaping) and a source (from which something flows outward). The same root is used for words describing exits, outputs, or comings and goings.
H8444.emploi: This word appears mainly in the precise descriptions of the boundaries of Israel and its tribes — in the books of Numbers, Joshua, and 1 Chronicles. Each time, it is about pointing exactly where a delimitation line "ends" or "terminates." The most frequent usage (about 15 times) is thus strictly geographical and technical. It is also found in poetry (Psalms 68:21) and wisdom (Proverbs 4:23) with more figurative nuances: the source of life, the power of God from which arrows spring, the thoughts of the heart. The word slightly changes hue depending on the context: sometimes it is purely spatial and determining, at other times it takes on a more inner or vital dimension.
H8444.portee: This word reminds us that God establishes precise boundaries and that everything has its rightful place in His plan — neither more nor less. In the narratives of land division, it highlights God's generosity in assigning each tribe a defined and secure territory. In Proverbs, the idea that the heart is the source of life invites us to guard our thoughts and intentions, for it is from there that everything else flows.

sens: To seek, examine carefully to discover or understand something
To traverse a territory to know its nature, resources, and dangers
To go in search of something, an active quest
Desire, personal inclination towards something
H8446.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is that of actively seeking by observing carefully. The ark of the covenant "seeks" a resting place as it moves ahead of the people (Numbers 10:33): it explores the path to find where to stop.

2. Very often, the word refers to the exploration of a territory. Moses sends men to "explore" the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:17), meaning to traverse it, observe its cities, its fertility, its inhabitants, and its defenses. These men spend forty days "exploring" before returning to report.

3. The word can also mean to set out in search, like a merchant who goes from place to place to seek goods to trade. In 1 Kings 10:15, we speak of "traders" who travel to do business.

4. Figuratively, "desires" in Numbers 15:39 refers to the inclinations, the wants that one "follows" — the heart that goes in search of personal satisfactions away from God's will.
H8446.origine: The Hebrew verb tur expresses the idea of moving to discover or investigate. It appears mainly in the Old Testament in narratives of exploration or observation. The image is that of a walker traversing a path, examining, going here and there to know. The nominal forms give the names of agents: the explorer, the spy, the trader. It is an active and concrete verb, always evoking a deliberate approach.
H8446.emploi: This verb appears 23 times in the Old Testament, particularly in Numbers in the account of the explorers sent to Canaan. Moses sends them to "explore" the land (Numbers 13:17), and this journey lasts forty days; their negative report leads to forty years of punishment in the desert. The image of exploration also recurs in the Psalms and Wisdom literature (Ecclesiastes, Job) where it denotes an intellectual or spiritual quest. In commercial contexts (1 Kings, 2 Chronicles), the participle designates traders on the road. The word can also apply to a curiosity of the heart diverted from good (Numbers 15:39).
H8446.portee: This word reminds us that knowing God's plan and dwelling in His promise requires courage and trust. The exploration of Canaan should have been an act of faith; instead, the explorers sought to see the obstacles rather than the promises. For the believer today, tur invites us to seek God and His will with seriousness and obedience, rather than being led by the "desires" of the natural heart.

sens: Succession, order, alternation in time
Row, line, sequence of aligned elements
Necklace, ornamental adornment
Braid or plait of hair
H8447.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of an alternation or succession: when several people must present themselves one after the other, each waits for their "turn." In Esther 2:12, each young woman waits for the moment assigned to her ("her turn") to present herself to King Ahasuerus; this turn comes after the twelve months of prescribed preparation.
2. By extension, the word designates a row or line of objects arranged in an orderly sequence. In Song of Solomon 1:10, the "necklaces" (literally the turns or rows) evoke jewelry arranged side by side around the neck, forming parallel lines of beauty.
3. A necklace or adornment is a succession of beads, links, or precious stones threaded and arranged in a circle; it is a neck ornament. In Song of Solomon 1:11, the poet promises to make "gold necklaces": these adornments composed of arranged elements create beauty and richness.
4. The word can also refer to a braid or plait (turn of hair), that is, a sequence of intertwined hair, forming an orderly arrangement.
H8447.origine: The Hebrew word תּוֹר (tor) comes from the root that expresses the idea of turning, forming a circle, or succession. The basic image is that of elements arranged in a line or loop: objects that follow one another, a necklace that wraps around, hair that is braided. The notion of order and succession is its semantic core.
H8447.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of beauty or order. Two occurrences are found in Esther 2, where it means the "turn" that each young woman awaits to be presented to the king: it is a regulated and expected succession. Two other occurrences are found in Song of Solomon 1, where it designates the "necklaces" — precious ornaments composed of arranged elements. The word always expresses either a temporal succession (wait your turn) or a spatial succession (row of beads or gold).
H8447.portee: This word reminds the reader that life has its times and orders: everyone has their moment, their place in the sequence of events. It also speaks of beauty as a harmonious arrangement — that of necklaces around the neck, that of established order. For the believer, it is a lesson in patience and trust in divine order.

sens: Braid or plait of hair or gold
Turn, spiral, winding
Way of acting, custom, usage
H8448.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a braid or plait, that is, hair or gold thread intertwined and wound together — the image of a succession of regular and repeated turns.
2. By extension, it evokes any winding or spiral: a turn that repeats, a spiral.
3. In a figurative sense, it means the usual way of behaving, the usage or custom. In 1 Chronicles 17:17, David says that God treats him "in the manner of men": that is, according to the way men ordinarily think and act, a comparison to show God's humility in condescending to the level of His creature.
H8448.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning, winding, making successive turns — like a thread that is wound or hair that is braided. This image of the repeated turn has naturally extended to the idea of habitual repetition, hence "custom" or "manner." The same family of words expresses winding and habit.
H8448.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Chronicles 17:17. David gives thanks to God, recognizing that the Lord speaks of him and looks at him "in the manner of men." This expression means that God adapts His language and kindness to human understanding — He speaks and acts in a way that man can comprehend, even though He is infinitely above any creature. It is a mark of divine grace.
H8448.portee: This word reminds the believer that God, although transcendent, condescends to come close to us and adapt His mode of action to our understanding. It invites recognition of the goodness and humility of God who condescends to speak and act according to ways we can understand, while remaining infinitely elevated above us.

sens: Bird with a soft and plaintive cry, smaller than a dove
Sacrificial victim for one who cannot afford a lamb or goat
Image of gentleness, innocence, and tenderness
Sign of the return of spring and new nature
H8449.detail:
1. The turtledove is a small bird with a melancholic song, belonging to the dove family but more delicate and petite. Its cry, which sets the tone for its presence in Scripture, evokes a certain tenderness. It can still be seen in the Middle East at the arrival of spring (Jeremiah 8:7: "The turtledove, the swallow, and the crane observe the time of their arrival").

2. The Lord accepted the turtledove as a ritual offering for those who could not afford to bring a lamb. In Leviticus 5:7, for the guilt offering, one could present "two turtledoves or two young pigeons" instead of a ewe or a goat. Similarly, a poor woman offered a turtledove for her purification (Leviticus 12:6 and 12:8).

3. The word also evokes innocence and gentleness: the Psalmist says, "Do not give the life of your turtledove to the beasts" (Psalms 74:19), personifying his defenseless people. This gentleness also characterizes the beloved in the Song: "The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land" (Song of Solomon 2:12).
H8449.origine: The Hebrew word תֹּור (tor) designates the bird in its nature — a gentle and domesticated animal. In the Old Testament, the turtledove is among the creatures that the Creator has endowed with a regular instinct: it knows when to migrate, it observes natural cycles. The word does not have a rich etymological family in Hebrew, but it is a stereotyped term for this specific bird, neither wild nor elusive, with a certain fragility.
H8449.emploi: The turtledove appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, first in a sacrificial context. In Genesis 15:9, the Lord asks Abraham for a turtledove and a young pigeon to seal the covenant. Then, throughout Leviticus and Numbers (more than 10 occurrences), it is the legal offering for those lacking resources: for guilt (5:7), the purification of women (12:6, 12:8), healing from leprosy (14:22, 14:30), purification after impurity (15:14, 15:29), and the fulfillment of the Nazarite vow (Numbers 6:10). It symbolizes the accessibility of worship even to the poorest. Outside of this framework, it embodies natural gentleness and innocence: the innocence of the vulnerable people (Psalms 74:19), beauty and purity (Song of Solomon 2:12), a reliable sign of the seasons (Jeremiah 8:7).
H8449.portee: The turtledove reveals God's heart for the poor and humble. Those who had nothing to offer but two birds could come to the sanctuary: God did not refuse their sacrifice. For the Christian, this reminds us that the Creator welcomes the offering of those who give little, provided they are sincere. Its natural innocence also speaks to those seeking to live in purity: it evokes a simple life, free from calculation and harshness.

sens: Animal for slaughter or sacrifice, adult male of the bovine species
Ox or young bull used in religious rituals and offerings
Image of brute strength and animal power
H8450.detail:
1. A bull is a domesticated animal raised for its work, meat, or bones, as can be understood in the context of offerings in Jerusalem (Ezra 6:9: "the burnt offerings of the God of heaven, young bulls, rams, and lambs"). It is the male of the bovine species, unlike cows or heifers.
2. In Israelite worship rituals, the bull is one of the major victims offered to the Lord: it was sacrificed during the dedication of the temple (Ezra 6:17: "one hundred bulls"), which shows its religious importance and the cost of the offering. The bull was considered a precious sacrifice.
3. In Daniel's dream, when King Nebuchadnezzar is humiliated, he is reduced to eating like the cattle of the grass (Daniel 4:33: "he ate grass like the cattle"), which emphasizes the king's degradation and lowering to the rank of a beast, expressing the loss of his human dignity.
H8450.origine: The Hebrew word תּוֹר (tor) is closely related to שׁוֹר (shor), which designates cattle or oxen in a broad sense, and appears from the earliest narratives in the Bible. In biblical Aramaic (the language of the book of Daniel and parts of Ezra), tor retains this same meaning. The basic image is that of a sturdy draft animal, capable of bearing the yoke and plowing the land.
H8450.emploi: The word tor appears mainly in the book of Ezra and in the book of Daniel, that is, in the Aramaic section of the biblical canon. In Ezra, it designates the bulls offered in sacrifice during the reconstruction of the temple: in 6:9, they are purchased for daily burnt offerings; in 6:17, one hundred are offered at the dedication; in 7:17, more are acquired for offerings. In Daniel 4 and 5, the word is used to compare the cursed king Nebuchadnezzar to a beast that grazes on grass: it is the image of his degradation and temporary animality. The context is always that of sacrifice, service, or humiliation.
H8450.portee: The bull reminds Christians that the worship of the living God required the Israelites to make true and costly offerings: to offer a bull was to deprive oneself of a precious possession. This reality invites reflection on the price of sacrifice and the generosity that God expected from His people. In the image of Nebuchadnezzar reduced to eating like an ox, we also see that God can humiliate the powerful: only the Most High "rules over the kingdom of men."

sens: Set of prescriptions and rules that God gives to His people
Direction, instruction, divine or human teaching
Specific prescriptions regarding a sacrifice or a specific ritual
Custom, established practice
The Law of Moses, given at Sinai
H8451.detail:
1. The law is primarily the set of prescriptions that God gave to Israel: these are not only prohibitions but a divine word that guides and directs the entire people. It encompasses moral commandments, worship rituals, and rules for communal living. In Deuteronomy 4:44, Moses presents "the law that Moses presented to the children of Israel."
2. The word also refers to instruction or teaching — the transmission of wisdom, a direction for living. This meaning appears when we speak of "the law of the Lord" as a living word that guides (Psalms 119:77: "your law is my delight").
3. In the books of Leviticus and Numbers, the term applies to each ritual prescription in particular: "the law of the sacrifice," "the law of purification." Each sacrifice has its own law (Leviticus 6:2, 7:1).
4. The word can simply designate a custom or an established practice, a recognized and followed way of doing things.
5. The term can finally refer to the Law of Moses as a whole, this foundational corpus given at Sinai and recited, taught, preserved by Israel through generations.
H8451.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to show," "to direct," or "to teach." The basic image is that of an instruction that orients and guides the one who receives it. This is why the word can designate both a specific law and a teaching, advice, or direction. In the Greek Septuagint (an ancient translation of the Hebrew Bible), this word is most often rendered by "nomos," the Greek word for "law."
H8451.emploi: The word appears 213 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Torah (the first five books) and in the history of Israel (historical books). It is particularly frequent in Deuteronomy, where Moses recalls and comments on the law given by God. The term primarily designates the set of divine prescriptions: the Law that God gave to Israel through Moses at Sinai, a law that the people must "observe" and "listen to." But it is also used for each particular prescription — each sacrifice has "its law" (Leviticus 6:2, 7:1), just as there is a law of purification, a law of vows, etc. Finally, the word can simply mean "instruction" or "direction," as when it is said that the law of the Lord is "His ways" that must be obeyed. The meaning often evolves according to the context, but always around the idea of a divine word that orients and governs.
H8451.portee: The law of God is not an oppressive constraint, but a word of wisdom and life: in Psalms 119:77, the one who meditates on it says that it "is his delight." It shows Israel — and every believer — how to please God and live according to His will. For an evangelical Christian, the law reveals the holy character of God and shows sin; it leads to recognizing our need for grace in Jesus Christ, who has fulfilled all righteousness.

sens: Teaching given to someone for their formation
Action of making something known to someone
Established way of acting, custom
H8452.detail:
1. Instruction is the teaching transmitted to someone for their formation and development. In 2 Samuel 7:19, David, amazed by God's promises, says: "You deign to instruct me" — God agrees to make known His plan for his house and his descendants, a privilege he receives with humility.
2. The word also designates the more general action of communicating knowledge or direction to someone. It is God who "deigns" to do this: the verb shows that it is an act of grace, of kindness.
3. The word can take on the meaning of custom or established way of acting, a rule of life that one receives and follows — which is why it is close to the meaning of law or order to be respected.
H8452.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of directing, showing, leading someone. Instruction is primarily the action of the one who guides: a teacher who teaches, a parent who trains their child, or God who reveals His will. The notion of law or custom derives from this: these are rules that "instruct" the one who receives them by showing them how to act.
H8452.emploi: This word appears once in the Segond translation in the precise sense of instruction or teaching received. In 2 Samuel 7:19, David expresses his amazement that the Lord deigns to instruct him — that is, to reveal the divine plan for his house. The context is one of personal revelation and divine grace: God grants David knowledge of his future. The word emphasizes the intimate relationship between God who instructs and the servant who receives this training or revelation.
H8452.portee: This entry invites the reader to meditate on the privilege of receiving instruction from God. Like David, who marvels that the Lord deigns to teach him, every believer can recognize that knowing God's will, understanding His promises and plan, is an act of grace. Divine instruction is never owed: it is a gift received with humility and gratitude.

sens: One who dwells in a country without being a citizen
A person attached to a household or family without being a full member
One who lives temporarily somewhere, just passing through
Man in relation to God: a tolerated guest, not an owner
H8453A.detail:
1. A resident alien is a person who lives in a country or place that is not their homeland. Abraham clearly states this in Genesis 23:4: "I am a stranger and a sojourner among you" — he has lived in Canaan for years, but remains a non-citizen without land ownership rights.
2. It also refers to one who lives under someone else's roof, engaged for service: in Leviticus 25:40, the poor person who sells themselves into servitude becomes "like a hired servant, like one who resides there" — they live in the house but do not own it.
3. The term sometimes simply designates an inhabitant of a region, one who resides there, like Elijah the Tishbite in 1 Kings 17:1, "one of the inhabitants of Gilead."
4. In a spiritual sense, the term summarizes the human condition before God: we are in Psalms 39:13 "strangers and sojourners" before the Lord, travelers without a permanent dwelling on this earth.
H8453A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that denotes the act of "sitting" or "dwelling" — hence the image of "living" somewhere. But it is not the resident-owner: it is one who is temporarily settled, tolerated but without deep roots. The word emphasizes this intermediate position between passing through and settling down, between the outside and the inside.
H8453A.emploi: The word appears primarily in the legal code of Leviticus (13 occurrences in total). The law of Israel carefully distinguishes between the native-born and the resident alien: the latter may work and live in Israel, but does not have access to the same rights — for example, they cannot eat the holy things of the sacrifice in Leviticus 22:10. However, in Leviticus 25:23 and 25:47, the law recognizes a protected legal status for them; they may be poor and sell themselves into servitude, but their condition changes. The word is also used simply to designate an inhabitant of a region (1 Kings 17:1). In a metaphorical sense, the Psalms apply it to all humanity before God.
H8453A.portee: This word reminds us that the true believer does not have a permanent dwelling on earth. Like Abraham and David, we are "strangers and residents": accepted by grace, living among men, but our citizenship is elsewhere. This comforts the believer who suffers from not having a place here below: it is normal, it is our calling. And it calls us to generosity towards the alien who dwells among us, since we ourselves live in spiritual exile.

sens: Deep and insightful knowledge of things
Ability to act with discernment and effectiveness
Lasting success resulting from wise action
Protection and salvation that God grants to the righteous
H8454.detail:
1. Wisdom here is not a mere accumulation of knowledge, but a deep understanding that grasps the reality of things. It is seeing clearly, understanding God's secret purposes. In Job 11:6, it is written that God reveals "the secrets of His wisdom": it is a knowledge that penetrates what is hidden.
2. This wisdom is always effective, productive: it leads to acting sensibly and succeeding. Proverbs 8:14 states, "Counsel and sound wisdom are mine," directly associating wisdom with the concrete fulfillment of plans.
3. The word also designates the lasting result of this applied wisdom — the success that persists, that asserts itself. When the "plans of the crafty are thwarted" (Job 5:12), it is due to the lack of this wisdom that produces true and stable success.
4. Wisdom becomes a form of salvation and protection from God: Proverbs 2:7 says that God "holds victory in store for the upright," where victory translates this same word, for divine wisdom is what preserves and delivers.
H8454.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of power, effectiveness, and accomplishment. It is a wisdom that is never inert or theoretical, but always active and fruitful. It stands in opposition to folly and impotence: where wisdom reigns, things come to a good end; where it is lacking, even the best intentions fail.
H8454.emploi: This word appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs) and in Isaiah. In Job, it often characterizes the unfathomable divine wisdom, which renders human calculation vain: God thwarts "the plans of the crafty" because His wisdom is incomparable. In Proverbs, it is a wisdom that God reserves for the righteous, a precious good that provides salvation and protection. Isaiah celebrates the "great wisdom" of God in His plans for the world. The word is also used for human wisdom: counsel, prudence, success in intelligent action.
H8454.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize that true wisdom comes from God alone and that it produces real fruits — protection, salvation, lasting accomplishment. It is never barren or vain. In the face of human plans that fail, divine wisdom remains stable and victorious. Cultivating this wisdom means learning to think like God, to see things as they truly are, and to act in a way that receives salvation and blessing.

sens: A combat weapon consisting of a heavy, thick stick, often flared at one end
H8455.detail: 1. A club is a primitive weapon of war: a sturdy stick, generally thick and weighted at its end, wielded to strike an opponent. The Hebrew word designates a heavy and formidable object. In the context of Job, where God describes the impressive power of Leviathan, this terrifying creature considers a club — a weapon that humans fear — as insignificant as a mere straw (Job 41:20). The image underscores the invulnerability and superhuman strength of this monster.
H8455.origine: The Hebrew word תּוֹתָח (totach) is infrequent in the Bible. It literally designates a striking combat object, likely related to the idea of a brutal blow. Hebrew uses other terms for weapons (sword, spear, bow), but this one specifically isolates the rudimentary weapon of close combat.
H8455.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Job 41:20. It is part of the marvelous discourse where God describes to the righteous Job the prodigious creatures He has created. In the face of Leviathan, a monster of colossal power, even a club — a symbol of human military strength — becomes ridiculous. This unique usage highlights the abyss between human fragility and the power of divine creatures.
H8455.portee: This word reminds us that every human weapon, every strength we accumulate, remains weak before the greatness of God and His creation. Job learns through this discourse the immensity of divine power that infinitely surpasses our abilities and defenses. It is an invitation to humility and trust in the One who rules over all things.

sens: To cut cleanly with a sharp tool
To remove or take away by cutting
To separate or prune parts of a plant
H8456.detail: 1. The verb "to cut" evokes the action of slicing something sharply and cleanly with an instrument like a sickle or blade. In Isaiah 18:5, it describes the gesture of the vine grower who cuts the branches with sickles: a clear and decisive action. 2. The word emphasizes not only the act of cutting but also the idea of removing or taking away what is cut — separating it from the rest. This is why the translation "removes" accompanies "cuts" in the same verse. 3. In the agricultural context of the vineyard, "to cut" means to prune, that is, to remove unnecessary or ripe branches to promote the grapes or harvest.
H8456.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that carries the idea of "to strike" or "to give a blow" to "remove" or "take away." The form used here (Hiphil) reinforces the idea: to make something be struck, that is, to cut or actively remove it. It is a rare verb in the Bible, appearing mainly in contexts of energetic and decisive action.
H8456.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 18:5. It is used in a concrete and agricultural sense: the vine grower preparing his vineyard before the harvest must cut the branches with a tool. It is a practical action verb, fitting into the description of agricultural work.
H8456.portee: For the reader, this verb reminds of the patient and intelligent work of the farmer: it is not enough to harvest; one must first prune, remove the unnecessary, and prepare the vineyard. The image suggests that preparation and discipline are essential before enjoying the fruit.

sens: Sexual relations outside of marriage, paid or not
Marital infidelity
Figuratively, abandonment of God for other gods or other alliances
H8457.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the act or state of a woman engaging in sexual relations for payment or favor, outside of marriage. It is the sin of sexual impurity in its most explicit form. Ezekiel 16:33 speaks of prostitution where "to all the prostitutes a fee is paid."
2. It extends to marital infidelity: Ezekiel 23:7 describes a married woman who "prostituted herself" by turning to other men. This is an abandonment of the fidelity bond that marriage imposes.
3. The text uses this word in a spiritual and figurative sense: the prophets describe Israel or Judah as an unfaithful wife who prostitutes herself by worshiping idols (Ezekiel 23:14: "She saw the images of Chaldeans and was attached to them"). The word then becomes an image of a breach of covenant with God.
H8457.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root זנה (zana), which means "to prostitute oneself" or "to be unfaithful." The form תַּזְנוּת (taznout) is the feminine noun that names the action itself. This root also appears in the verb and in names of people who prostitute themselves. In biblical Hebrew, it always carries a strong moral connotation: it designates not only an act but a deviation from the path or a serious infidelity.
H8457.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in Ezekiel (16 times in chapters 16 and 23). These two chapters are oracles of judgment where the prophet describes Jerusalem (chapter 16) and Samaria/Oholiba (chapter 23) as unfaithful women who have prostituted themselves by worshiping the idols of neighboring nations: Egypt, Assyria, Chaldea. The word gradually takes on a legal and spiritual meaning: it names not only sexual impurity but the betrayal of the covenant that God made with Israel. The passages show God enumerating this infidelity as a reason for judgment and punishment.
H8457.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that infidelity toward God is described in the Bible with the language of the most serious sexual sin. It is not a simple mistake or a consequence-free deviation: it is a breach of the covenant bond, a betrayal of love. For the believer, this underscores the importance of remaining attached to God alone and not being seduced by the "idols" of the world. It is also a call to repentance to return to faithfulness.

sens: Direction, guidance given by someone wise or prudent
Judicious advice, practical wisdom for action
Well-considered plan or project
Ability to discern and advise wisely
Tactical or strategic skill
H8458.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the direction or guidance that someone wise communicates: it is the art of showing the right path. In Job 37:12, God directs the clouds according to His "plans," that is, His thoughtful and ordered designs.
2. It also means wise counsel, the wise word that a thoughtful person offers to someone in need. The one who listens increases their knowledge and acquires "skill" (Proverbs 1:5): prudence is the ability to discern what to do.
3. The word also expresses a plan or project conceived with reflection. The "plans" of the righteous are equity, while those of the wicked are deceit (Proverbs 12:5): what one intends to do reflects who one is.
4. In political or military context, prudence becomes the art of governing or waging war wisely. Proverbs 20:18 and 24:6 call for waging war with "prudence": it is deploying strategic thought to succeed.
H8458.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to invent" or "to weave," with the idea of tying together, combining. It appears mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs) where one reflects on the right way to live and advise. Prudence is not innate: it is what one learns by listening to the wise.
H8458.emploi: The word appears six times, only in the wisdom books (Job and Proverbs). It designates either divine direction (Job 37:12, where God guides natural phenomena) or human reflection: prudence is what the people who collapse lack (Proverbs 11:14), what one acquires by listening to the wise (Proverbs 1:5), what characterizes the thoughts of the righteous (Proverbs 12:5), or what is needed to succeed, particularly in war (Proverbs 20:18, 24:6). It stands in opposition to folly and dishonesty.
H8458.portee: This word invites the believer not to act lightly. The Bible calls for seeking prudence, that is, to reflect, listen to the wise, and organize one's thoughts and plans before acting. It is recognizing that true intelligence, far from being spontaneous, requires work and humility. For the Christian, it is also learning that God governs the world with wisdom and deserves our trust.

sens: Levite, ancestor of Samuel
H8459.detail: Thohu is a Levite, a member of the tribe chosen for the service of worship in Israel. He appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 1:1, as a link in an important genealogy: he is the son of Tsuph and the father of Elihu. This name carries significant genealogical meaning, as Thohu is the great-grandfather of Samuel, the great prophet and judge of Israel who will mark a turning point in the spiritual history of his people.
H8459.origine: The name Thohu means "humble" or "lowly." Although not well documented in the Bible, this name reflects the spiritual orientation of the Levitical families: it emphasizes humility before God, a characteristic valued among the temple servants. The genealogical context shows a pious lineage from which several important servants of worship arise.
H8459.emploi: Thohu is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 1:1, where he appears in the genealogy of Elkana. This genealogy places him in the Levitical lineage that leads to Samuel, thus establishing the religious and priestly legitimacy of a family called to play a decisive role in the history of Israel during the period of the united monarchy. His appearance in this genealogical verse, though brief, places him within a lineage of servants of God.

sens: In a lower position relative to something
Sheltered by, protected by
Below, in the lower region of
H8460.detail:
1. The word designates the position of a person or thing placed beneath another: the animals sheltered "under" the shade of a great tree, meaning in the space covered by its branches (Daniel 4:12).
2. It also expresses the state of being protected or covered by something: the creatures find refuge "under" the branches and foliage of the cosmic tree (Daniel 4:21).
3. More broadly, it indicates a region or totality considered as inferior: "all the kingdoms that are under heaven" refers to the entirety of the earthly world, in contrast to heaven (Daniel 7:27). The gods will disappear "from under" the heavens, meaning from the earthly domain (Jeremiah 10:11).
H8460.origine: This Aramaic word is a form of the Hebrew word תַּחַת (ta.chat), which also expresses the inferior position and covering. The family of words shares the fundamental image of what is below, hidden, or sheltered. In Aramaic, this preposition is formed with the vowel e at the beginning, which slightly distinguishes it from its Hebrew equivalent but retains the same directive meaning.
H8460.emploi: This preposition appears 5 times in the Aramaic passages of the Bible: 2 times in Jeremiah 10:11 and Daniel, 3 times in the dream of the great tree (Daniel 4:12, 4:14, 4:21) and 1 time in the vision of the kingdoms (Daniel 7:27). It is used for concrete geographical or spatial positions (under the shade of the tree, under the branches) and for abstract sets (under the heavens, meaning over the entire earth). Its role is constant: to situate a reality in the lower region or hidden in relation to something greater or higher.
H8460.portee: This preposition, through its use in the dream of the great tree, reminds that every living creature depends on a higher source that nourishes and protects it. It invites the reader to meditate on the hierarchy of realities: there exists an order, beings, and domains that are "under" others, and this subordination is not humiliating but just. In the final vision (Daniel 7:27), it emphasizes that all the kingdoms of the world will be given to the people of God.

sens: Warrior of David, one of the most powerful military leaders
Descendant of the clan of Hachmon or Tahchemon
H8461.detail:
1. The Tachkemonite is Josheb-Basshebeth, one of the greatest warriors in the service of King David. He is presented as one of the chief officers (2 Samuel 23:8) and his strength is legendary: he wielded his spear against eight hundred men whom he killed at one time. He is a warrior whose military exploits are unparalleled.

2. This title "Tachkemonite" also designates his belonging to a clan or family, that of Hachmon or Tahchemon. It is a designation that connects this warrior to an ancient warrior lineage, known for its power and skill in battle.
H8461.origine: The word tachkemonite comes from the name Hachmon or Tahchemon, to which a suffix is added indicating belonging or descent (as when we say "a Benjamite" for someone from the tribe of Benjamin). The name Hachmon itself could mean "one who makes wise" or "wisdom" in Hebrew, but the true importance here is genealogical: this title indicates that Josheb-Basshebeth belongs to the family or clan of the Hachmonites.
H8461.emploi: Josheb-Basshebeth the Tachkemonite appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:8, in the list of "mighty men" in the service of David. This list enumerates the greatest warriors of David, those who contributed to his victories and the stability of his reign. The Tachkemonite occupies the first place, which underscores his rank and exceptional reputation among the king's elite soldiers.
H8461.portee: This warrior reminds the reader that strength and courage are also gifts from God, used in the service of a king after His own heart. The mention of these "mighty men" shows that God strengthens His servants and builds His victories not by magic, but through men of faith and valor. It is an invitation to see how natural and spiritual gifts serve the will of God.

sens: The moment when something begins, its start
The first time something occurs
At the start of a period, a season
Previously, in the past (with a preposition)
H8462.detail:
1. The moment when something begins, its start: This is the initial moment of an action or event. Genesis 13:3 speaks of the place where Abraham had his tent "at the beginning," meaning at the start of his journeys in Canaan.
2. The first time something occurs: This refers to a particular occurrence, the first among others. In Genesis 43:20, Jacob's sons say: "We have already gone down once to buy food," recalling their first trip.
3. At the start of a period, a season: The word marks the starting point of a duration. Ruth 1:22 specifies that Ruth and Naomi arrived in Bethlehem "at the beginning of the barley harvest," at the time when the harvest begins.
4. Previously, in the past (with a preposition): With a preposition, it refers to an earlier moment, to what happened before. Isaiah 1:26 speaks of judges "as they were at the beginning," meaning in an idealized past.
H8462.origine: This Hebrew root evokes the beginning, the starting point of all things. It is linked to the idea of what is "first" or "original." The root appears in composition with other words in the Bible to indicate various beginnings: the beginning of a harvest, a word, a reign. It is a fundamental word for expressing the notion of initial time.
H8462.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and wisdom narratives. It is used to mark the concrete beginning of events: the beginning of a harvest (Ruth 1:22), of a journey (Genesis 13:3), or of rain (2 Samuel 21:10). It can also refer to a first occurrence or a first attempt (Genesis 43:20). With prepositions, it expresses the idea of "since the beginning" or "as before," allowing for comparison of a present state to a previous one (Isaiah 1:26). The word is rarely used in the context of absolute or cosmic beginnings: it remains linked to concrete and historical beginnings.
H8462.portee: This word reminds us that every action, every event has a beginning. For the believer, this raises a question: who or what is truly "at the beginning"? Isaiah 1:26 invites us to return to a just beginning — when God will restore Jerusalem as a city of justice. This speaks to us of God's desire to restore what has been lost, and of the renewal possible in our lives through Him.

sens: Physical affliction that weakens or destroys the body
State of intense suffering due to an illness
Wasting of the body from hunger or exhaustion
H8463.detail: 1. A disease is an affliction of the body that strikes and makes it sick: this is how God strikes a land with diseases (Deuteronomy 29:22), thereby showing His judgment. 2. The disease can also cause violent and intolerable suffering: this is what King Joram endures, as his entrails come out due to the severity of his illness over two years (2 Chronicles 21:19). 3. By extension, anything that consumes the body — hunger in particular — is also called a "disease," as it reduces the body to nothing just as a disease would (Jeremiah 14:18; Jeremiah 16:4).
H8463.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means to be sick or weak. It designates the pathological state of the body, this natural fragility of the flesh that makes it vulnerable to disease. It is a concrete term: it speaks of what the body endures, not an abstract notion.
H8463.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the context of divine judgment or extreme suffering. In Deuteronomy 29:22, diseases are among the plagues sent by the Lord upon the rebellious land. In 2 Chronicles 21:19, they characterize a pathological and inglorious agony. But Psalm 103:3 reverses the meaning: it is the Lord who heals diseases, showing His mercy towards the people. In the passages from Jeremiah, the word expands to also designate wasting due to famine, as the devastation is similar to that of a destructive disease.
H8463.portee: This word reminds the believer that disease is a reality of the fallen world, but also that the Lord has power over it: He strikes with disease, but He also heals (Psalms 103:3). It is an invitation to see in everything that consumes the body an opportunity to turn to God, the sole master of life and health.

sens: An unclean bird according to the law of Moses
Probably a large nocturnal raptor or a bird related to the ostrich
H8464.detail:
1. In the law of Moses, the owl is among the birds that are not to be eaten, as they are ritually unclean. It is listed alongside the ostrich and other raptors: it is a creature that the God of Israel has marked as forbidden at the table of God's people (Leviticus 11:16; Deuteronomy 14:15).
2. The exact word refers to a bird that hunts at night or a strange creature: perhaps a large owl or a screech owl, or possibly even a bird that has become extinct whose exact name escapes us today. The important thing for the biblical reader is not the precise zoological species, but the principle: it is an unclean bird, and the Israelite must keep away from it.
H8464.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes tenacity or seizing. The owl, a nocturnal animal that watches and seizes its prey in the darkness, bears this name that reflects its character as a hunter. Like other birds of prey in the Levitical list, it belongs to a family of animals marked by violent hunting or predatory behavior, which explains their impurity in the law.
H8464.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in lists of unclean animals: once in Leviticus 11:16 and once in Deuteronomy 14:15, which repeat the same prohibition with very similar wording. These two passages are parallel lists of creatures that cannot be eaten or touched. The bird is always presented among other predatory birds (the ostrich, the hawk) and appears without additional commentary: its impurity is self-evident within the framework of the Mosaic law.
H8464.portee: The owl reminds the believer that the law of Moses taught Israel to dedicate themselves to God through every action of daily life, including the choice of what to eat. By prohibiting predatory animals, the law guided Israel to cultivate a difference, a visible holiness in the details of life. For the Christian reader, this illustrates how God educated His people to reflect on moral images: the violence and tenacity of the nocturnal hunter were not suitable for a people called to justice and mercy.

sens: Son of Ephraim and ancestor of a family of Israel
H8465G.detail: Tachan is a man of the tribe of Ephraim, son of Telah and father of a lineage bearing his name. He is mentioned in the census of the people of Israel in the wilderness, where Moses enumerates the families descended from the sons of Ephraim (Numbers 26:35). From him descends the family of the Tachanites, whose name perpetuates his memory among the tribes of Israel.
H8465G.origine: The name Tachan literally means "camp." It bears the trace of an ancestor rooted in the nomadic history of Israel. His descendants are called Tachanites, formed by the addition of the common Hebrew suffix of filiation.
H8465G.emploi: Tachan appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:35, during the census that Moses conducts in the plains of Moab, before entering Canaan. He is listed among the sons of Ephraim whose families structure the tribe. This genealogical text establishes the order of the clans and legitimizes Ephraim's territorial inheritance at the time of the conquest.

sens: Man of the tribe of Ephraim
Son of Telah and father of Ladan
Ancestor of an Ephraimite family
H8465H.detail:
1. Tachan is a man belonging to the tribe of Ephraim, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Ephraim, the son of Joseph.
2. He is the son of Telah and the father of Ladan (also called Leadan), thus forming an important link in the genealogical chain of his tribe.
3. His family constitutes a recognized lineage among the Ephraimites, whose history continues through his descendants mentioned in the genealogical records of Israel.
H8465H.origine: The name Tachan comes from the Hebrew תַּחַן (tachan), whose original meaning is "camp." This name evokes the idea of a dwelling or established place of residence. The root is found in several biblical passages related to the encampment of the Israelites during the Exodus. Tachan thus bears a name that recalls the memory of God's people's encampments in the desert.
H8465H.emploi: Tachan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the first book of Chronicles, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim. This genealogy lists the descendants of Ephraim, son of Joseph, and places Tachan in the lineage: he succeeds his father Telah and precedes his son Ladan. This genealogical passage is a reference document for the structure and history of the tribes of Israel before and during the period of the divided monarchy.

sens: Place where an army temporarily settles
Act of setting up a camp
State of temporary installation of a troop
H8466.detail:
1. The encampment is the very place where soldiers pitch their tents and settle to sleep and rest, away from battle. In 2 Kings 6:8, the king of Syria sets up his encampments to prepare for war against Israel — these are the precise locations where his army settles.
2. The word also designates the very action of setting up this camp, the moment when the army stops and organizes its space for the night or for an extended halt.
3. It is a temporary state: the encampment is never permanent, unlike a city or a fortress. It is the place of passage for an army on the move.
H8466.origine: The word comes from the root חנה ("to stop, to spend the night"), which expresses the idea of pitching tents. It is the natural vocabulary of the Old Testament to describe the installation of nomadic or moving armies — like the Israelites in the desert who "pitched their encampment" step by step.
