H8466.emploi: The word appears only once in 2 Kings 6:8, in a story where the prophet Elisha reveals to the king of Israel the secret plans of the king of Syria: "The king of Syria was waging war against Israel; he took counsel with his servants, and said: I will camp in such and such a place." The usage here is military and strategic: it refers to specific locations that the enemy chooses to concentrate its forces.
H8466.portee: This word reminds of the vulnerability of an army on the move. Even the mightiest must stop, sleep, and organize their survival — which makes them accessible to God's intervention. In the account of Kings, it is by revealing the secret encampments that the Lord protects Israel, showing that God knows and dominates the plans of His people's enemies.

sens: urgent request addressed to God
appeal to God's goodness and mercy
humble prayer accompanied by tears
H8467.detail:
1. The word designates an intense and respectful request addressed to God, often in a moment of need or distress. It is an act of prayer that expresses the urgency of the heart. When King Solomon "raises his supplication" before the Lord in his newly constructed temple (1 Kings 9:3), he begs God to favorably listen to the prayers of the people.
2. Supplication carries an expectation of grace: it not only asks to be heard but to be welcomed with kindness. The psalmist cries out: "O God! Give ear to my prayer, and do not hide yourself from my supplications!" (Psalms 55:2), imploring that God does not reject his call. It is seeking favor and mercy.
3. It is distinguished from a simple word: it is a prayer that insists, that returns with humility. Jeremiah "supplicates" the king not to send him back to death (Jeremiah 38:26), placing all his trust in a respectful request.
H8467.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "bending towards" or "asking earnestly." The family of this word includes other terms of prayer and request. In biblical Hebrew, supplication is always a humble approach before someone greater than oneself, particularly before God who can grant or refuse.
H8467.emploi: This word appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the books of prayer (Psalms), religious history (Kings, Chronicles), and prophecy (Jeremiah, Daniel). It is very frequent in contexts of royal prayer: Solomon "prays and supplicates" God for the consecration of the temple (1 Kings 8:28, 8:30, 8:38, 8:45, 8:49, 8:52, 8:54). It also appears when men of God implore forgiveness or help: Ezra supplicates God while confessing the sins of the people (Ezra 9:8), and Jeremiah supplicates the king several times in his distress (Jeremiah 37:20, 38:26). Sometimes "supplication" is simply alongside "prayer," both terms reinforcing the idea of a sincere and urgent request.
H8467.portee: Supplication teaches us that there is no shame in humbly asking God for what we need. It encourages the believer to address God not as a stranger, but as someone who hopes to be listened to favorably. It is also a reminder that God delights in answering the sincere prayers of those who seek Him.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H8468.detail: Thechinna is a character in the genealogy of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Eshton and the father of Ir-Nahash, "the city of Nachasch" (1 Chronicles 4:12). His name means "supplication" in Hebrew, but it is unknown whether this meaning reflects the circumstances of his birth or if it is merely a family legacy. He belongs to the descendants of Reca, a group of Judahite families.
H8468.origine: The name Thechinna comes from the Hebrew תְּחִנָּה (techinah), which means "supplication" or "pleading prayer." The root is חנן (chanan), which evokes the idea of asking graciously, of imploring divine favor. This name belongs to the tradition of theophoric or significant names in the Old Testament, where a person's name could reflect a prayer or parental vow.
H8468.emploi: Thechinna appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:12, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. He is presented as the son of Eshton and the father of Ir-Nahash. This brief mention places him in the time of the Divided Monarchy in Israel. Like most names in this genealogy, his exact historical role remains unknown; it is only known that he belongs to a Judahite lineage established in the territory of Judah.

sens: urgent request, earnest prayer addressed to God
appeal for pity or compassion
act of imploring with humility and insistence
H8469.detail: 1. Supplication is a prayer that comes from the heart with urgency and insistence. It is not a simple word, but a living call, often marked by emotion and distress. The psalms illustrate this well: "O Lord, hear my prayer, give ear to my supplications" (Psalms 143:1), where the psalmist almost repeats the same idea to show the intensity of his request. 2. It is a request born from the awareness of one's need and dependence on God. The poor, one who has nothing else to offer, makes his supplications (Proverbs 18:23). Jeremiah speaks of supplications poured out in tears (Jeremiah 31:9): it is a cry from the depths of the soul. 3. Supplication implies an attitude of humility and trust: one presents oneself before God not demanding a right, but begging, that is, imploring His grace. Daniel, at the moment of confessing the sins of the people, presents his supplications "not because of our righteousness, but because of [Your] great mercies" (Daniel 9:18).
H8469.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be gracious, to plead, to implore." It is from the same family as other Hebrew words concerning grace and prayer. The initial image is that of someone turning to a superior person, often the king or God, to request an act of pity or favor. It is the language of the weak before the powerful.
H8469.emploi: This word appears 18 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the Psalms, the Prophets, and the wisdom books. It mainly recurs in collective or individual prayers addressed to God: David, Jeremiah, and Daniel use it to express their fervent requests. In 2 Chronicles 6:21, Solomon asks God to hear the supplications of the people. In the Psalms (28:6, 116:1, 143:1), the psalmist affirms that God hears and answers supplications. Jeremiah 31:9 shows Israel returning to God "weeping" amid his supplications. Daniel 9 presents supplication as accompanying confession and fasting, a sign of sincere repentance.
H8469.portee: Supplication teaches the believer that prayer is not primarily a polite word or a list of requests, but a relationship: it is turning to God with sincerity, urgency, and humility. It revalues the one who prays by placing him in the right attitude: not as an equal negotiating, but as someone who depends on divine grace. It also invites us to believe that God truly hears and responds to those who supplicate Him with all their heart.

sens: Descendants of Tahan, son of Ephraim
H8470.detail: The Thachanites are the descendants of Tahan, a man of the tribe of Ephraim living during the time of Egypt and the desert. This clan name appears only once in Numbers 26:35, during the census of Israel in the desert. Tahan had brothers Shuthelah, Becher, Ezer, Elead, and Beriah, all sons of Ephraim.
H8470.origine: Thachanites comes from the name Tahan (Thachan in French), which means "you will decline" or "you will bend." This name designates a son of Ephraim, and the suffix -ites indicates belonging to this family clan, according to the biblical usage of names of tribes and families.
H8470.emploi: The Thachanites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:35, during the enumeration of the families of Ephraim in the desert. This census lists the different clans descended from the sons of Ephraim, and the Thachanites are included as one of these officially recognized families. This mention reminds us that each clan had a specific identity and place within the structure of Israel.

sens: fortified city in the Egyptian delta, in northern Egypt
H8471.detail: Tachpanès is an important Egyptian city located in the Nile delta about 29 kilometers east-southeast of Tanis. It served as a fortress and administrative center. The Bible mentions it primarily as a place of exile: after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., Jews fled there in disobedience to the prophet Jeremiah, who had instructed them to remain in Judah (Jeremiah 43:7). The prophet received divine messages there (Jeremiah 43:8) and performed a symbolic act before the Pharaoh's house (Jeremiah 43:9).
H8471.origine: The Hebrew name תַּחְפַּנְחֵס (Tachpanès) corresponds to the ancient Egyptian name. Its etymology suggests "you will fill the hands with pity," although the connection to the historical city is uncertain. It is a transliteration of the Egyptian name preserved in the Hebrew text.
H8471.emploi: Tachpanès appears 7 times in the Bible, only in the prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel. It is mentioned primarily in connection with the exile of the Jews in Egypt after 586 B.C. Jeremiah, who had prophesied that the people would be exiled, receives divine messages there against those who take refuge (Jeremiah 43:7-9). It is also listed among the Egyptian cities struck by divine judgment (Ezekiel 30:18). The prophet performs a symbolic act of judgment at the Pharaoh's palace gate, signifying that Nebuchadnezzar will conquer Egypt.
H8471.portee: Tachpanès reminds readers that fleeing from God's will to seemingly safe places does not protect one from God's judgment. It also symbolizes how God speaks to His people even in exile and how His word will be fulfilled everywhere, even in foreign lands. It is a call to obedience rather than flight.

sens: Queen of Egypt during the time of King Solomon
H8472.detail: Thachpenès is an Egyptian queen who lived during the time of David and Solomon. She is the wife of the Pharaoh of Egypt and plays a role in the diplomatic relations between Egypt and Israel. In 1 Kings 11:19-20, she intervenes to offer one of her sisters in marriage to Hadad, an Edomite prince who fled Israel and found refuge in Egypt. Her sister gives birth to a son, Genubath, whom Thachpenès herself raises in the Pharaoh's royal house, treating him as one of the princes of Egypt. This gesture shows her influence and generosity within the Egyptian royal family.
H8472.origine: The name Thachpenès means "woman of the king" or "wife of the king" in Egyptian. It designates the royal queen, companion of the Pharaoh during the period of ancient Egypt when Israel was already established as a united kingdom under David and Solomon.
H8472.emploi: Thachpenès appears twice in the biblical text, only in 1 Kings 11:19-20. She is mentioned in the context where the Pharaoh of Egypt welcomes Hadad, the exiled Edomite prince, and proposes marriage to Thachpenès's sister. The text shows her personally intervening to raise her sister's son, Genubath, indicating her high status and authority in the Pharaoh's house.

sens: Protective garment made from interwoven threads
Flexible armor covering the torso and arms
By extension, reinforced opening or edge of a fabric
H8473.detail:
1. This word designates a tightly woven garment made by interlacing threads very closely and regularly. The image is that of a flexible armor that protects the body by weaving the thread very densely, like a mail. In Exodus 28:32 and 39:23, it describes the opening of the high priest's ephod, which had to be securely bordered to avoid tearing: it is therefore a densely woven border, like that of a mail shirt, to reinforce the fragile area.
2. In a general sense, this word applies to any flexible woven armor that covers the torso and protects the fighter. It is a common type of military equipment in the ancient Near East.
3. By extension, the word also designates any reinforced edge or hem of a fabric, woven to be very strong and to prevent the garment from tearing: this is the meaning of the term in the description of the priest's ephod.
H8473.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of crossing, interlacing, or weaving together. The starting image is that of threads crossed and tied together very densely to form a solid and impermeable mesh. This type of garment was common in the ancient Near Eastern army, where the mail shirt provided light but effective protection against blades and arrows.
H8473.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Exodus, in chapters 28 and 39. In these two passages, it does not refer to military armor, but to the technical description of the ephod, the priestly garment of the high priest. The opening intended for the head was reinforced by a densely woven border, "like the opening of a mail shirt," so that the garment would remain intact and not tear during repeated use. This detail shows that the priest's garment was made with care and durability.
H8473.portee: This word reminds us that in Israel's worship, the holy ceremony was also a matter of practical care and durability. The high priest's garment was a centerpiece, constructed with the utmost attention, so that divine service could be performed with dignity and without interruption. It is a detail that shows how faith also involves faithfulness to well-made and durable things.

sens: To measure oneself against someone in a fight or competition
To experience inner agitation, a vehement ardor
H8474.detail:
1. To struggle means to confront an opponent, to fight or compete with them. Jeremiah asks the prophet: "If you run with footmen and they weary you, how will you contend with horses?" (Jeremiah 12:5). The image is that of a competition where one must exert oneself, show strength and perseverance to avoid being defeated.
2. The word also describes an inner passion that stirs and burns within. When the Lord reproaches a king for his "passion for the cedar," He speaks of that fire that consumes someone, an ardor, a desire that torments (Jeremiah 22:15). It is less about confronting someone else than about battling the effervescence of one's own emotions.
H8474.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that carries the idea of burning, of igniting. At its core is the image of fire and heat: an anger that flares up, a desire that boils within. Heat produces agitation, first in the heart, then in all behavior. This is why the word means both "to struggle" and "passion": it is about a burning energy, whether directed against an opponent or towards oneself.
H8474.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In both cases, it expresses an inner ardor or confrontation. In Jeremiah 12:5, it denotes the physical and moral struggle that must be faced — a trial that requires effort. In Jeremiah 22:15, it describes a king's consumerist passion, his ardent desire for luxury. Both usages show that this term speaks of forces that stir, whether aimed at an opponent or seeking an object of satisfaction.
H8474.portee: Jeremiah reminds the distressed prophet that true Christian life is not won without struggle: it requires endurance and courage in the face of obstacles. The mention of a king's "passion" for the cedar also warns the believer: having a heart on fire for true values — justice and equity — is better than being consumed by desires for wealth and comfort.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy
H8475.detail: Tahréa is a member of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogy of Saul. He is the son of Micah and the brother of Pithon, Melech, and Ahaz. The same person is referred to as Tarea in 1 Chronicles 8:35, while Tahréa appears in 1 Chronicles 9:41: these are two names or variants of the same individual.
H8475.origine: The name Tahréa means "cunning" or "sly" in Hebrew, evoking a form of cleverness or sagacity. He belongs to the royal lineage of Saul, an ancestor who will play a central role in the history of Israel.
H8475.emploi: Tahréa is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:41, in the context of the genealogy of Saul during the period of the united monarchy. This mention places the character within the family tree of the tribe of Benjamin and the first king of Israel. The fact that he is also referred to as Tarea in 1 Chronicles 8:35 shows that biblical genealogies sometimes used different forms of the same name or that some individuals had multiple names.

sens: Skin or hide of a marine animal
Material for covering and protecting sacred objects
H8476.detail:
1. The word refers to the skin or hide of a marine animal, probably a dolphin, seal, or a similar animal from which a waterproof and durable material was derived. In Exodus 25:5, "dolphin skins" are requested among the materials for constructing the tabernacle.
2. This skin served as a protective covering for worship objects: the ark of the covenant, the altar, and the sanctuary utensils were to be wrapped in coverings made of this waterproof material, as indicated by the prescriptions in Numbers 4:6 and 4:10, which speak of "covering of dolphin skins" placed over the blue draperies.
H8476.origine: The Hebrew word tachash likely refers to a marine animal whose thick, waterproof skin was highly valued. Ancient versions often translated it as "dolphin" or "dugong." It has no certified equivalent in current fauna and may refer to an extinct species. The biblical context shows that it was a valuable material, suitable for sacred constructions.
H8476.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Bible, exclusively in passages that prescribe the construction of the tabernacle (Exodus 25 to 39) and the transport of its objects (Numbers 4). It is a material listed among the precious materials that the Israelites were to bring: red skins, acacia wood, gold, silver, bronze. In Numbers 4, the Levites who transported the sanctuary objects were to wrap them in dolphin skin coverings and then drape them in blue, which protected the consecrated items. A unique occurrence in Ezekiel 16:10 mentions shoes made of this material, symbolizing beauty and well-being. It is a material exclusively associated with holy things.
H8476.portee: This word reminds us that God prescribed in minute detail how to construct and protect His sanctuary. The choice of rare and waterproof materials to wrap the ark and sacred objects shows the seriousness and respect due to the things of God. It invites us to meditate on the holiness of the divine presence and on how we treat what belongs to the Lord.

sens: Son of Nahor and his concubine Reumah
Nephew of Abraham
Brother of Tebah, Gaham, and Maacah
H8477.detail: Tahasch is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the descendants of Nahor, Abraham's brother, are listed. He is presented as the son that Nahor had with his concubine Reumah (Genesis 22:24). His name appears in a family genealogy that dates back to the time of the Patriarchs, in the days of Abraham. Tahasch is part of the children born from this union and is counted among the ancestors of the Aramean peoples.
H8477.origine: The name Tahasch literally means "dugong" (a marine mammal), an image that may evoke a strong or remarkable creature. In the context of patriarchal genealogies, this name, like many others on this list, reflects the connections of Abraham's people with the populations of the ancient Near East, likely those of Aram-Naharaim.
H8477.emploi: Tahasch appears only once in the entire Bible, in Genesis 22:24, in the genealogy that lists the twelve children of Nahor. The text places him after the experience of Isaac's sacrifice and serves to establish the familial ties of Abraham and his family. This brief mention is part of a passage that documents the descendants of the Patriarchs and the peoples that arose from them.

sens: The space or region that is below, under something
The lower part of an object or structure
In place of something or someone, as a replacement
Under the control or domination of someone
At the foot of, near something (in an idiomatic expression)
H8478G.detail:
1. The physical space located below, under something: it is the opposite of above. Genesis 1:7 speaks of the waters that are below the expanse of the heavens, opposed to those that are above.
2. The lower part of an object: thus in Exodus 26:33, the veil is placed below the clasps, meaning lower than them, in the Tabernacle.
3. In place of, as a replacement: when something is placed "underneath" another, it replaces it. This can also mean "for the sake of" or "because of".
4. Under power or domination: in Psalms 47:4, God subdues nations, meaning He places them under His control, in a position of submission.
5. At the foot of, near: in certain fixed expressions, the word denotes the immediate proximity of a place or person (Judges 4:5, Deborah sits "under the palm tree").
H8478G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of what is low, inferior. It is a fundamental spatial word in Hebrew. The same root appears in other words denoting lowness or lowering. The basic meaning is physical and concrete: what is below, and from there it extends figuratively to express submission, control, and substitution.
H8478G.emploi: This word is among the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible (214 occurrences). It primarily denotes physical position: the waters below the heavens (Genesis 1:7), the beams of the Tabernacle (Exodus 26:19-25). It is also used to indicate what is hidden or buried (Joshua 7:21, where the stolen goods are hidden "underneath" the tent). The word is also used to express domination: God places enemies under the feet of His people (Psalms 47:4). Finally, it often means "in place of," "in exchange for," an important notion in sacrifices and redemptions. Deuteronomy 4:39 uses it to contrast the high heaven and the low earth.
H8478G.portee: This word reminds every believer that the order of the world has meaning: the high and the low, the superior and the inferior, the dominant and the submissive. It speaks of God's power that brings down His enemies and exalts His people. It is also a word of grace when it expresses substitution: someone else takes "our place," a crucial concept for understanding the sacrifice of Christ.

sens: The space occupied by someone or something, from which it is absent
To take the position, function, or role of someone else
To serve as compensation, exchange, or payment for something
Below, under something
In relation to, opposite to
H8478H.detail:
1. The space where someone or something stood before being removed or separated: for example, after God took a rib from Adam, the flesh closed "in its place" (Genesis 2:21), meaning at the spot it occupied.
2. To occupy the position, function, or authority of another: when a king dies, his son reigns "in his place" (1 Kings 15:8), taking his throne and power. This is the most frequent meaning in the accounts of the kings.
3. To serve as a replacement, equivalent, or payment in exchange: if someone injures an animal, he must pay "in place of" the animal (Exodus 21:36) — what he gives as compensation. Or when Judas offers himself as a slave "in place of" Benjamin (Genesis 44:33), he substitutes for him.
4. Under, below: an inferior or submissive position, often figuratively used to express domination or suffering ("under the yoke", "oppressed").
5. In front of, in relation to: used to locate something in relation to another thing or person.
H8478H.origine: The Hebrew word תַּחַת (tachat) comes from a root meaning "to be under" or "to be low." It is fundamentally a spatial word that designates what is below. Its primary, concrete meaning ("under") has naturally extended to the meaning of "in place of," as one who takes the place of someone else puts themselves in their position — they occupy it. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (Septuagint), this word is often rendered by ἀντί (anti), which also carries the idea of position and exchange.
H8478H.emploi: This word appears about 170 times in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is very common in the accounts of the kings of Israel and Judah (1 and 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles), where it regularly describes succession: a son "reigns in place of" his father. It is also found in legislative texts, notably in the Law of retaliation (Exodus 21:23-25), where it expresses the principle of equivalent compensation ("a life for a life"). In the accounts of Genesis, it can mean a substitution or replacement, as when Seth is born "in place of" Abel, or when a ram is offered "in place of" Isaac. Its usage is concrete and direct: it rarely carries a figurative meaning in the Hebrew Bible.
H8478H.portee: This word reminds us of the divine order of the world: each being, each function has its assigned place. It also emphasizes the biblical idea of equivalence and compensation: one life, one debt, one service can substitute for another. For the believer, it evokes the important notion of substitution — a central idea at the heart of Christ's sacrifice, who offers himself in place of all men. Understanding this word helps to grasp how the Bible thinks about exchange and replacement.

sens: The lower part of something, what is underneath
The location where something or someone stands, rests, or remains
The position occupied by someone before them, their role or function
Under the action, authority, or weight of something
H8478I.detail:
1. The lower part, the underside of something: this is the most concrete meaning, that of foundation or base. In Exodus 10:23, during the plague of darkness, "no one rose from their place" literally describes the ground where one stands.
2. The location where one is, where one dwells or remains: this can be a geographical position or a given location. In Leviticus 13:28, the priest examines whether a burn mark "has remained in the same place," meaning at the same spot on the skin.
3. The position occupied by someone else, what is called a substitution or replacement: when something takes the place of something else. In Joshua 6:5, "each in front of themselves" suggests that each advances to their place in line.
4. Under the influence or weight of something, expressing submission or oppression: an image of what crushes or masters. In Job 40:7, God "crushes the wicked on the spot," meaning keeps them on the ground by His strength.
H8478I.origine: The Hebrew word תַּחַת (tachat) comes from a root expressing the idea of being low or underneath. Its basic image is that of foundation, ground, what supports or holds up. It is found in a whole family of Hebrew words designating the underside, the low, the depth. The word can also express exchange or substitution, since what is placed "under" something can replace or supplement it.
H8478I.emploi: The word תַּחַת (tachat) appears 28 times in the provided texts, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Chronicles), the Law (Exodus, Leviticus), and the wisdom books (Job). Its most frequent uses simply designate the place or position where one stands or dwells (Exodus 10:23, 2 Samuel 2:23, 1 Chronicles 5:22). The word also extends to the idea of collapse or destruction, as when "the wall will collapse" in Joshua 6:5. In a figurative context, it evokes oppression or being crushed under a power (Job 40:7), thus expressing submission or domination. This versatile word therefore carries meanings ranging from concrete location to the moral condition of subjugation.
H8478I.portee: Understanding this word helps to grasp how the Bible speaks of stability, rest, and position before God. When the text says one remains "in their place," it describes a state of presence and establishment. When it speaks of "crushing," the word reveals how God masters evil and imposes His order. It is a key to perceiving the biblical importance of positioning: where one stands, who dominates us, where we find our rest or submission.

sens: In the literal sense: what is underneath, below something
In the sense of substitution: in place of, instead of, in exchange for
Indicating the cause or reason: because, due to the fact that, for the reason that
Indicating the consequence: so that, in such a way as to
H8478J.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the lower part, what is underneath: this is its most concrete meaning and its basic image. This spatial notion extends to the idea of what one stands on, or what supports.

2. From this arises the sense of substitution or equivalence: "in place of," "instead of." When a slave is struck in the eye and loses it, he is freed "for the price" (that is, in compensation, in place of the damage) of his eye (Exodus 21:26). It is an exchange: something replaces another thing.

3. The causal sense is the most frequent in the Bible: the word expresses the reason or motive for an action. "Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat" (2 Chronicles 21:12) explains divine judgment. "Because I seek good" (Psalms 38:21) states why one becomes an enemy. The reason is what "supports" or "foundations" an action — a spatial image that has become logical.

4. Sometimes the word introduces a consequence or purpose: "so that," "in order that." This nuance depends on the context and the verbs used.
H8478J.origine: The Hebrew word תַּחַת (tachat) comes from a root that designates the lower space, inferior. Its primary image is spatial: what is underneath. From this root, words of the same family have formed that retain this notion of lower space or low position. The Greek of the Old Testament often translates this word as ἀντί (anti, "in place of, in exchange for") or ὑπό (hypo, "under"), which shows how the Greek also understands the transition from spatial meaning to the meaning of substitution or cause — since the cause, like the foundation, is what "supports" from below.
H8478J.emploi: This word appears 23 times in the provided Hebrew Bible, especially in the Pentateuch (Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles). Its most common use is conjunctive: it introduces the reason for an action or judgment. Thus, Numbers 25:13 explains the priestly covenant "because he [Phinehas] was zealous"; 2 Chronicles 21:12 enumerates the wrongs of the king "because you have not walked in the ways of your fathers." Less often, it marks exchange or compensation: "for the price of his eye" (Exodus 21:26). The pure spatial sense ("under," "beneath") is present but less visible in these conjunctive uses. The nuance varies slightly depending on the context: sometimes it is a simple cause ("why"), sometimes a broader cause ("due to the fact that"), sometimes an equivalence ("in place of").
H8478J.portee: For the Christian reader, this seemingly trivial word opens a deep understanding: it shows how the Bible reasons in chains of causes. Understanding when God acts "because" reveals His justice — it is never arbitrary, always founded on reason. Moreover, the link between the spatial meaning ("beneath") and the causal meaning ("because") invites one to see that reason, faith, and justice are like foundations: they support, they uphold all of life. It is a discreet yet powerful lesson on the coherence of God.

sens: The lower part, what is underneath
What is under the hand, under someone's control
The act of dominating, ruling over
The position where one stands, the place occupied
In place of, in exchange for, instead of
H8478K.detail:
1. The lower part, what is underneath: this is the concrete and spatial meaning of the word. It designates what is below, under something. In 2 Kings 17:7, Israel came out "from under the hand of Pharaoh," meaning it escaped the oppressive power of the king of Egypt — "underneath" here refers to the heavy grip, the domination that held them.
2. What is under the hand, under someone's control: this is the domain, territory, or subjects over which authority is exercised. In 2 Kings 8:20 and 2 Chronicles 21:8, Edom revolts "against the authority of Judah": authority designates sovereignty, the right to command and govern. What was "under" the control of Judah wants to be free.
3. The act of dominating, ruling over: in a political and military sense. When speaking of the "authority" of a king, one describes his right to govern, the power he exercises over a people or territory. It is this power that is exercised "from above" over what is "below."
4. The position where one stands, the place occupied: the word can designate the physical or social position of a person, their rank, their station. It is the place where someone stands and from which they exercise their power.
5. In place of, in exchange for, instead of: this is the conjunctive and prepositional use of the word, which marks a substitution or compensation. Instead of this, we have that; in return for this, we receive that.
H8478K.origine: The word comes from the root "tacht" which literally means "to be low," "to be underneath." The starting image is spatial: what is below, what is under something or someone. From this derives the idea of dependence, submission: if you are underneath, you are under the authority of the one who is above. In Hebrew, this same word takes different forms depending on the context — preposition, noun, conjunction — but always retains this central image of what is "below" or "under control." It is a very ancient and very common word throughout the Hebrew Bible.
H8478K.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the biblical uses noted, especially in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the prophets. It is primarily used to designate political and royal authority. The kings of Judah exercise their "authority" (or "dominion") over neighboring peoples; when Edom revolts, it is because it rejects being "under" this authority. The word also describes deliverance: Israel comes "from under the hand of Pharaoh" when God frees it from slavery (Exodus, 2 Kings 13:5). The word conveys the idea of grip, heavy oppression: being "under the hand" of someone means being submitted, dependent, deprived of freedom. It is a key word for discussing kingship, subjection, and liberation.
H8478K.portee: This word helps the reader understand what authority means in the Bible: it is not an abstract power, but a concrete domination, a "hand" that weighs upon the people. It also sheds light on the notion of sin as rebellion: to revolt "against authority" is to refuse to stay in one's place, to refuse to obey the one who reigns. And it shows that true biblical freedom is not the absence of all authority, but the escape from a bad authority — not freeing oneself from God, but freeing oneself from tyrants, and finding authentic freedom under the authority of the true God.

sens: To be placed under, beneath
To place oneself under someone's authority, to obey
To swear by placing one's hand under another's thigh
H8478L.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a physical position: to be underneath, below something. The image is that of what is below, at the bottom, underneath something else.
2. Figuratively, it expresses subordination and obedience to someone: to place oneself under the authority of a person, acknowledging their right to command. When the leaders and the sons of David "submitted" to King Solomon (1 Chronicles 29:24), they recognized his royal authority.
3. The word also evokes the gesture of the ancient oath: placing one's hand under someone's thigh while swearing (Genesis 24:2 and 24:9), a solemn gesture to affirm that one will keep their promise. This body position — hand under the thigh — symbolizes the acceptance of domination and commitment to the one to whom one swears.
H8478L.origine: The Hebrew word תַּחַת comes from a root that evokes what is below, underneath. It belongs to the family of Hebrew prepositions and adverbs of place. Its primary meaning is spatial — the place that is under another — but the Bible quickly employs it figuratively to express the idea of submission and servitude. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it often corresponds to words that indicate subordination.
H8478L.emploi: The word تحت appears 4 times in the provided references. It first describes the gesture of the oath: Abraham instructs his servant to place his hand "under his thigh" to swear to find a wife for Isaac (Genesis 24:2), and the servant does so (Genesis 24:9). Jacob also asks Joseph: "Put your hand under my thigh" before making him swear something (Genesis 47:29). In 1 Chronicles 29:24, the leaders "submit" to Solomon, which shows the transition from the physical meaning of the gesture to the figurative meaning of submission. In all these cases, the word expresses either the position of the body (the hand under the thigh) or the idea of recognizing authority.
H8478L.portee: This word reminds the reader that submission to God and to those He establishes involves a serious and solemn commitment. The ancient gesture of placing the hand under the thigh to swear shows that our promises and obedience are not mere words: they engage our whole being. It is a lesson on faithfulness and respect for one's word.

sens: Station where Israel camped during the Exodus
H8480G.detail:
1. Tahath is a stop on the journey of the people of Israel through the desert, between the departure from Egypt and the arrival in the Promised Land. It is listed among the encampments enumerated in the book of Numbers: Israel arrives there coming from Makhéloth and departs towards Tarach (Numbers 33:26-27). It is one of the many stations where the people stopped to rest and resupply during these forty years of wandering.
2. The name means "station" or "stopping place" in Hebrew, evoking a place where one stops to camp. It is a geographical name that designates a specific location on the route taken by the Israelites under the leadership of Moses.
H8480G.origine: The name means "station" or "stopping place" in Hebrew, evoking a place where one stops to camp. It is a geographical name that designates a specific location on the route taken by the Israelites under the leadership of Moses.
H8480G.emploi: Tahath appears only twice in the Bible, both in the passage of Numbers 33 that enumerates the forty-two encampments of Israel in the desert. This account precisely lists each stage of the journey, from the departure from Egypt to the plains of Moab. Tahath occupies a modest place in this enumeration, but it illustrates how God guided His people through the desert, step by step.
H8480G.portee: This mention of Tahath reminds the reader that every moment of Israel's journey to the Promised Land was counted and directed by God. It symbolizes God's constant guidance and faithfulness, nourishing and protecting His people even in the difficult moments of the desert.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, son of Assir and father of Uriel
Levite of the tribe of Levi, son of Assir and father of Zephaniah
H8480H.detail: Thachath is a name borne by at least two Levites of the tribe of Levi during the time of the divided monarchy. The first is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:24 as the son of Assir and father of Uriel, part of the priestly lineage of the Kohathites. A second Levite of the same name, also son of Assir, is cited in 1 Chronicles 6:37 as the father of Zephaniah. It is possible that these two mentions refer to the same person, or two different Levites bearing the same name in the priestly genealogy.
H8480H.origine: The name Thachath means "station" in Hebrew, evoking a place or stopping point. This name may also refer to a station of the people of Israel in the desert, according to tradition. The name reflects the importance of stations or stops in the history of Israel.
H8480H.emploi: Thachath appears twice in Scripture, both in 1 Chronicles 6, in the genealogies of the Kohathite Levites. In 1 Chronicles 6:24, he is presented as the son of Assir and father of Uriel, fitting into a long priestly lineage. In 1 Chronicles 6:37, another Levite bearing the same name appears in a similar genealogy, as the father of Zephaniah. These genealogies reconstruct the succession of Levite leaders during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Ephraim during the time of the divided monarchy
Levite of the family of Kohath
H8480I.detail:
1. Thachath is a name borne by several men in ancient Israel. The most well-known is a descendant of Ephraim living at the time when the kingdom was divided: he is the son of Bered and the father of Elead, part of a long genealogy listed in 1 Chronicles 7:20.
2. The name Thachath also designates Levites of the family of Kohath, temple clerks, although the biblical genealogies that mention them are uncertain regarding their precise distinctions.
H8480I.origine: The name Thachath means "station" in Hebrew, likely evoking a stopping place or point of halt. This name reflects the context of the travels and stations of the people of Israel in the desert and during their movements, a common practice in biblical onomastics to name children after significant events or places.
H8480I.emploi: Thachath appears only once in the Segond, in 1 Chronicles 7:20, in the genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim. He is presented as a link in a long succession of generations connecting Ephraim himself to his descendants during the time of the divided monarchy. This genealogical passage aims to establish the continuity of the people of Israel and the persistence of tribal family lines despite the political divisions of the kingdom.

sens: Man of the tribe of Ephraim during the time of the divided monarchy
H8480J.detail: Thachath is a name borne by several characters in the genealogy of Ephraim. The one mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:20 is a descendant of the tribe of Ephraim, son of Elead and father of Zabad, living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. The name means "station" and evokes a place of rest or stop — an image that suits a genealogy anchoring the Israelites in their history.
H8480J.origine: The name Thachath comes from the Hebrew root meaning "place," "station," or "beneath": the idea of stopping or taking position. This biblical name belongs to the genealogy of Ephraim and reflects the onomastic traditions of Israelite families in the Old Testament, where names often carried significance related to places or memorable actions.
H8480J.emploi: Thachath is a genealogical character mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 7:20. He appears in the list of descendants of Ephraim, recorded in the genealogical chain that traces back to the founder of the tribe. Several other characters bear this name in the Old Testament (notably among the Kohathite Levites), but the one cited here stands out for his place in the Ephraimite genealogy. His appearance in Chronicles reflects the chronicler's interest in the continuity of the Ephraim lineage.

sens: Located at a lower level, lower in altitude
H8481G.detail: 1. This word literally means "lower" or "situated below." It describes a geographical position: Beth-Horon the Lower was a city built at a lower altitude than Beth-Horon the Upper, its twin located on the heights (Joshua 16:3). The two cities formed a fortified complex whose defenses Solomon strengthened (1 Kings 9:17).
H8481G.origine: The Hebrew word tachton comes from the root tachat (תַּחַת), which means "under" or "below." It is an adjective that simply expresses a spatial relationship: that which is lower or situated beneath something else. The same root appears in many Hebrew words expressing a position below.
H8481G.emploi: This word appears only five times in the Bible, always to refer to Beth-Horon the Lower. This locality, mentioned in the books of Joshua, Kings, and Chronicles, was a strategic city of the tribe of Benjamin, fortified by Solomon. It was thus distinguished from Beth-Horon the Upper by its location on the slopes rather than at the summit. The term does not describe a moral or spiritual quality, but only a geographical position.

sens: Located below, downwards
Occupying a lower level in a multi-story building
At the lowest level
H8481H.detail:
1. The word simply describes what is found below, downwards, in contrast to what is high or superior. In 1 Kings 6:6, Solomon builds the temple with three stories: "the lower story was five cubits wide," which is the one at the very bottom of the building.
2. In the architectural descriptions of the temple in Ezekiel, the word regularly designates the intermediate or lower story of a multi-level structure. The lower chambers are more spacious than those in the middle and upper levels, as explained in Ezekiel 42:5: "The upper chambers were narrower than the lower ones."
3. The word can also qualify what is at the lowest level, the ground or the lower area of a complex. In Ezekiel 40:19, it measures "from the lower gate to the inner court," thus designating the lower level of the temple.
H8481H.origine: The Hebrew word תַּחְתּוֹן (tachton) comes from the root תַּחַת (tachat), which means "under, below." It is an adjective formed to express what is situated in the lower position. This same root is found in words of the same family designating what is beneath, down, or hidden. The fundamental image is that of the space located below, in contrast to that which is above.
H8481H.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Bible, mainly in the detailed descriptions of Ezekiel's temple and in the account of Solomon's temple construction in 1 Kings. It always designates a spatial position: either a story or a lower area in an architectural structure. In 1 Kings 6:6, it characterizes the lowest story of Solomon's temple. In chapters 40 to 42 of Ezekiel, which describe the future temple very precisely, the term regularly recurs to distinguish the different levels of chambers and doors. The word has no spiritual or moral significance: it is a simple spatial, objective, and architectural description.
H8481H.portee: This word shows us how the Bible accurately describes the concrete details of the temple and its constructions. For the Christian, it reminds us that God is interested in the order, structure, and beauty of places dedicated to His worship. The meticulous descriptions of the temple invite the reader to meditate on the holiness of God's house and the importance of what is reserved for His service.

sens: What is located below, underneath
What is beneath a surface, in the interior of the earth or water
What is lower in position or rank
The abyss, the pit, the depths of death and the realm of the dead
H8482.detail:
1. The word first designates what is localized below, in an inferior position: the lower stories of a house (Genesis 6:16 speaks of the three stories of the ark, including the lower one), or the water sources that flow lower in the terrain (Joshua 15:19).
2. It also evokes what sinks into the depth: the deep layers of the earth or the abysses of water. The trees of Lebanon descend into the depths of the earth when God brings them down (Ezekiel 31:16).
3. The word can qualify what is lower in rank or importance, like the lower millstone (the one below) of a mill (Job 41:15).
4. Figuratively, it designates the depths of the realm of the dead, the abyss where the dead descend. The psalmist cries from the depths of the pit (Psalms 88:7; Lamentations 3:55), and the dead descend into the depths of the realm of the dead (Ezekiel 32:18).
H8482.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of what is low, lowered, sunk down. The same root generates verbal forms meaning "to lower" or "to be lowered." The image is that of movement downwards, of the depth that opens beneath our feet: what is "takhtî" belongs to the lower layers, to the hidden areas of what surrounds us.
H8482.emploi: This word appears nineteen times in the Hebrew Bible, especially among poets (Psalms, Job, Lamentations) and in the prophets (Ezekiel, Isaiah). It first designates concrete and architectural realities (the stories of a building), then the deep parts of nature (water, earth). As one progresses through the Bible, especially in Ezekiel, the word acquires a spiritual and eschatological significance: it describes the realm of the dead, those depths where the deceased descend and where God can also cast the wicked. The contrast with what is high (heaven, surface) becomes a language of the human condition before God.
H8482.portee: This word invites the believer to become aware of hidden and deep realities: it reminds us that beneath the surface of the visible world exist unknown depths where God acts and where His judgment reigns. For those who suffer, the cry "from the depths of the pit" (Psalms 88:7) becomes an authentic language of distress before God, and the assurance that the Lord hears even those who have descended into the depths of misfortune. It is also a call to vigilance: not to forget that human life has abysses and limits that only God knows.

sens: Place located near Gilead, east of the Jordan
H8483.detail: Thachthim-Hodschi is a region mentioned only once in the Bible, during the census of Israel ordered by King David. It is located in Gilead, in the lands situated east of the Jordan, in a northeastern border area of Israel.
H8483.origine: The name literally means "lower moon" or "new moon" in Hebrew (from "tachti" = lower or inferior, and "chodesh" = month or new moon). The exact origin of this geographical name remains uncertain, but it likely designates a mountainous region or a valley in Gilead.
H8483.emploi: Thachthim-Hodschi appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 24:6. The context is that of the census of the people of Israel commanded by David: the king's officers traverse the territory to count the men of fighting age, and their route leads them to Thachthim-Hodschi, in the region of Gilead, before continuing to Dan-Jaan and up to the vicinity of Sidon.

sens: Central space between two ends or limits
Intermediate floor in a building
Intermediate moment in a progression
Court or interior space of a building
H8484.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of a space located between two ends: thus, the middle bar of the Tabernacle runs "from one end to the other" (Exodus 26:28), which means it connects both sides by passing through the center.
2. In a multi-level building, the middle refers to the intermediate floor: in the Temple, the middle floor was six cubits wide, while the lower floor was five and the third seven (1 Kings 6:6).
3. This word can also refer to an intermediate moment in time: the middle watch refers to the second of the three watches of the night, that of midnight (Judges 7:19).
4. Finally, it can evoke an interior space, a court: the middle court is the central space of the Temple (2 Kings 20:4).
H8484.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that fundamentally means "to be in the center" or "to divide in two." It belongs to the family of words describing position or location. Its initial image is that of a point or place equidistant from both ends, making it primarily a spatial word.
H8484.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in architectural descriptions and indications of time or place. It is frequently used in the books of Kings and Ezekiel to describe the floors of the Temple and its courts. In Exodus, it qualifies the bar of the Tabernacle. In Judges 7:19, it marks a specific moment of the night. The word remains always concrete: it describes a real position or location, never abstract.
H8484.portee: This word reminds us of the order and structure that God has given to His sanctuary: each part of the Tabernacle and the Temple had its precise place, including what was in the middle. It invites the reader to see that the presence of God rests on meticulous harmony, where nothing is left to chance.

sens: Son of Ishmael
Desert region inhabited by the descendants of Tema
H8485G.detail:
1. Tema is the ninth son that Ishmael had with his Egyptian wife. He appears in the genealogical lists of Genesis and Chronicles alongside his brothers, notably Nebaioth, Kedar, Massa, and others. His name means "desert" in Hebrew, evoking the nomadic lifestyle of these ancient Near Eastern peoples.
2. Beyond the person, Tema also designates the desert region that his descendants occupied and inhabited. This land, located in Arabia, was known as the territory of the Temanites, descended from this son of Ishmael. The proper name thus extends from the patriarch to his posterity and the lands they controlled.
H8485G.origine: The name Tema comes from Hebrew and literally means "desert." This root evokes the arid and desolate environment of the Arabian Near East where the descendants of Ishmael lived. Ishmael himself, the rejected son of Abraham, fathered twelve sons who became the fathers of the Arab peoples; Tema is one of the most significant.
H8485G.emploi: Tema appears twice in the Bible: in Genesis 25:15 and in 1 Chronicles 1:30, both places in a list of the twelve sons of Ishmael. These two parallel passages each provide the complete genealogy of Ishmael, establishing Tema as the ninth son. The Bible does not recount any specific actions of Tema himself, but names him among the ancestors of the Arab peoples. The historical Tema was an important trading center in the Arabian desert, and the name has persisted as a designation for both a person and a region.

sens: Desert region of Arabia
Nomadic people or tribe of the Arabian desert
H8485H.detail: 1. Tema is a desert region in Northeast Arabia, known for its trade routes and caravans. In Job 6:19, the caravans of Tema catch the eye, evoking the long convoys of merchants that traversed these arid lands. 2. The term also designates the people or tribe that inhabited this region. In Isaiah 21:14, the inhabitants of the land of Tema are people living in the desert, capable of bringing bread to the fugitives, showing a community established in these areas. In Jeremiah 25:23, Tema is listed among the peoples that will face divine judgment, alongside other Arab nations like Dedan and Buz.
H8485H.origine: Tema is the name of a son of Ishmael according to Genesis 25:15. It designates both the person and the region he established in the desert of Arabia. The name seems linked to a real region, historically known as an important oasis on the trade routes of the Arabian desert, located in Northern Arabia.
H8485H.emploi: Tema appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 6:19, it is mentioned as a region through which trade caravans pass, highlighting its importance in the ancient Near Eastern exchange network. In Isaiah 21:14, it is presented as an inhabited land, whose residents are organized enough to provide aid to fugitives. In Jeremiah 25:23, Tema is included in a list of peoples subjected to God's judgment, indicating its status as a recognizable nation in the eyes of the Israelites.

sens: Cardinal point to the south
Region or southern side
Direction towards the south
Wind from the south
H8486.detail:
1. The south is the cardinal point located to the south, the direction opposite to north. It is one of the four fundamental directions for orientation (along with north, east, and west). In the tabernacle, the Israelites establish structures "on the south side" (Exodus 26:18).
2. The south also designates a region, a territory, or a geographical area located towards the south. The "southern side" of the tabernacle is mentioned (Numbers 3:29) or the "south side" of a piece of land (Joshua 12:3).
3. The word expresses a direction of movement: going south means heading towards the south. This meaning is common when indicating how to walk or where to look.
4. The south can also refer to the south wind, the sirocco. This dry and hot wind comes from the southern desert. In the Song of Solomon, the "sirocco" is called to blow over the garden (Song of Solomon 4:16), probably for the fragrance it brings.
H8486.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that literally means "right" or "right hand." For an ancient Israelite turning towards the east (the direction of the rising sun), the south is to his right, hence this name. The same root produces words for "right-handed" and "south." In the Greek Old Testament, this word is often translated by a term meaning "south" or "southern region."
H8486.emploi: The word south appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in geographical and architectural descriptions. It is found especially in Exodus and Numbers, where it specifies the location of the tabernacle structures (the boards, the sides of the camp). It also designates the southern regions of Israel and beyond (Job 9:9 mentions the "southern regions" of heaven). The word is also used for winds (Song of Solomon 4:16, Psalms 78:26), and even poetically to indicate a cosmic direction (Zechariah 6:6). Its meaning remains constant: the south, whether in terms of terrestrial or celestial orientation, geography, or movement.
H8486.portee: Understanding that the Bible uses cardinal points to structure space and provide landmarks helps visualize the sacred places of worship. The south is not just an abstract direction: it is a side of the tabernacle, an inhabited region, a wind that comes from somewhere. This reminds us that biblical faith is embodied in concrete places and tangible experiences of the created world.

sens: Son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau
Tribe leader or prince in the genealogy of Edom
Region of Edom inhabited by the descendants of Teman, renowned for its wisdom
H8487G.detail:
1. Teman is the first son of Eliphaz, who is himself the firstborn son of Esau (Genesis 36:11). He appears in the genealogies of the descendants of Esau, the founder of Edom, a brother nation to the Israelites.
2. The name Teman also refers to a tribe leader or prince of the people of Edom (Genesis 36:15). The biblical genealogies list him among the important leaders descended from Esau.
3. The region of Teman, also called Thêmân or Teman, became the territory inhabited by his descendants in Edom, to the east and south of the land of Israel. This region was known in antiquity for the wisdom of its inhabitants, particularly its wise counselors.
H8487G.origine: The name Teman means "south" in Hebrew, reflecting its geographical location in the southern part of Edom. The word is related to the Hebrew root that designates the direction of south. Teman is not only a person but also the name of the region he inhabited, which bore his name in later traditions.
H8487G.emploi: Teman appears five times in the Old Testament, exclusively in the genealogies of Esau in Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1. He is consistently presented as the son of Eliphaz and a tribe leader. The genealogical lists name him among the other sons of Eliphaz (Omar, Zepho, Gaetham, Kenaz) and highlight his status as an Edomite chief or prince. Although mentioned infrequently, the region of Teman gains historical and biblical significance: it becomes famous for its sages, as evidenced by later prophetic allusions in the Old Testament.

sens: Region of the south, territory of the Themanitis
Habitat of the descendants of Teman, son of Eliphaz
Region renowned for the wisdom of its inhabitants
H8487H.detail: 1. Teman is the name of a geographical region located east of Idumea (that is, the territory of Edom), in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. The name itself means "south" in Hebrew, indicating the direction where this land was located in relation to Jerusalem. 2. The region was populated by the descendants of Teman, who was a son of Eliphaz, himself the son of Esau. These inhabitants, the Temanites, formed a distinct community within the Edomite people (Jeremiah 49:7-20; Amos 1:12). 3. Teman was particularly known in the ancient world as a center of wisdom: biblical texts explicitly mention the renowned wisdom of its inhabitants, to the point that the prophet Jeremiah questions, "Is there no more wisdom in Teman?" (Jeremiah 49:7), suggesting that this reputation was well established.
H8487H.origine: The name Teman comes from Hebrew and literally means "south." It is derived from the root that designates the southern direction. Teman was the son of Eliphaz and the grandson of Esau, which explains why this territory bore the name of its founding ancestor. The inhabitants of the region were called "Temanites" (תֵּימָנִי) and formed a recognizable group within Edom.
H8487H.emploi: Teman appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the prophets announcing judgment against Edom. The prophet Jeremiah mentions it twice (49:7 and 49:20) when speaking of the punishments that struck the region. Amos (1:12) and Obadiah (1:9) also cite it to announce fire and devastation. Ezekiel (25:13) refers to it when describing the extension of divine judgment against Edom "from Teman to Dedan." In Habakkuk (3:3), the name appears more lyrically, as a geographical reference in a theophanic vision. In each occurrence, Teman represents either a center of wisdom that cannot be ignored or a region that was struck to punish the Edomites.
H8487H.portee: Teman reminds us that human wisdom, however renowned it may be, cannot withstand the judgment of God. Its inhabitants, reputed for their intelligence, could not escape the condemnation pronounced against Edom for its sins. This region illustrates how the wealth and reputation of a nation, even based on real excellence, will not preserve it if it turns away from the Lord.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H8488.detail: Temeni is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:6. He is the son of Ashhur and Naarah. He has brothers Ahuzzam, Hepher, and Achashthari, all born of Naarah. The genealogical context shows that Ashhur had two wives: Naarah, the mother of Temeni and his brothers, and another woman who bore him Zerah, Izhar, Ethnan, and Koz.
H8488.origine: The name Temeni means "from the south" or "southern" in Hebrew, derived from the root that evokes the direction of south. It is a descriptive name, likely given to this child to mark a characteristic or circumstance of his birth or origin.
H8488.emploi: Temeni appears only once in the Holy Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 4:6, in a genealogical list of the tribe of Judah. This passage enumerates the descendants of Ashhur during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel. His inclusion in this genealogy indicates that he was a man of some importance in his tribe, worthy of genealogical remembrance.

sens: Inhabitant of Teman, a region in the southeast of Idumea
Descendant of Teman, grandson of Esau
Member of the royal or noble lineage of Edom
H8489.detail:
1. Temanite designates someone from Teman, a region located east of Idumea (the ancient land of Esau). Husham, king of Edom, came "from the land of the Temanites" (Genesis 36:34).
2. The term refers to a direct descendant of Teman, who was himself the grandson of Esau and a chief of Edom. It is a prestigious lineage in the genealogy of the neighboring kingdoms of Israel.
3. In the book of Job, Eliphaz is presented as "of Teman": he is a wise man and a friend of Job, suggesting that the Temanites enjoyed a reputation for wisdom and respectability in the ancient Near East (Job 2:11; Job 4:1).
H8489.origine: Temanite comes from the name Teman (Hebrew תֵּימָן), whose root literally means "the south" or "toward the south." Teman was the grandson of Esau and a chief (duke) of Edom. The suffix -ite indicates belonging to a people or region, as in many biblical names. The word designates both a geographical region (the land of the Temanites) and the inhabitants of that land.
H8489.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily concentrated in two contexts. First, in the genealogy of Edom (Genesis 36:34; 1 Chronicles 1:45), where it reminds us that the Temanites provided a king to Edom. Secondly, and most importantly, in the book of Job, where Eliphaz, Job's friend, is consistently referred to as "Eliphaz of Teman" (Job 2:11; 4:1; 15:1; 22:1; 42:7; 42:9). This repetition emphasizes Eliphaz's identity and geographical origin, associating the Temanites with the wisdom tradition of the ancient world.
H8489.portee: Eliphaz embodies external and carnal wisdom: although respected and from a renowned region, he fails to understand the mysterious ways of God with Job. His status as a Temanite, a member of a prestigious lineage of Edom, shows that human wisdom, even the most honorable, is insufficient to grasp the designs of God. It is a lesson on the limits of reason in the face of the divine mystery.

sens: Vertical structure that supports or rises
Set of things aligned vertically and closely together
Figurative element suggesting strength and stability
H8490.detail: 1. A column is a vertical structure, often cylindrical or pillar-shaped, that supports a building or stands alone. In Joel 2:30, the "columns of smoke" evoke plumes of smoke rising straight to the sky, dense and well-formed. 2. The word also refers to a group of elements aligned vertically, closely packed together, like troops advancing in formation. In Song of Solomon 3:6, the beloved rises from the desert "like columns of smoke," an image of majestic and visible presence. 3. Figuratively, a column symbolizes strength, stability, and importance: it supports the sky or captivates the gaze because it stands firmly and impressively. This image reinforces the idea of grandeur and solidity.
H8490.origine: The Hebrew word תִּימָרָה (timarah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of rising or pointing upward. Its primary image is that of an imposing vertical structure, like a palm trunk standing upright. The name may also evoke the aspect of the palm at its flared top, since an ancient column was often crowned with a capital (upper element) that widened like the fronds of a palm tree.
H8490.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in vision or poetry. In Song of Solomon 3:6, it describes the beloved's ascent from the desert under the poetic image of "columns of smoke," mingled with vapors of myrrh and incense, evoking a splendid and visible presence. In Joel 2:30, the "columns of smoke" are a sign of the coming divine judgment, a fearsome manifestation of celestial and earthly wonders. In both cases, the word reinforces the image of something rising firmly, seen from afar, and striking the imagination.
H8490.portee: This image of columns of smoke reminds us that the divine presence is visible and imposing: it rises before the eyes of all. For the believer, it speaks of God's majesty manifesting itself unmistakably, whether in the beauty of communion (Song of Solomon) or in the power of judgment (Joel). It invites us not to ignore the signs of God, but to recognize and take them into account.

sens: Inhabitant of a city or region called Hittite
H8491.detail: 1. Hittite designates a man from a locality named Hittite. It is an ethnic nickname, as often found in the Bible to denote a person's geographical origin. Jocha, brother of Jediael, bears this designation in the list of David's warriors (1 Chronicles 11:45).
H8491.origine: The word Hittite is formed from the name of a place, Hittite, to which a suffix indicating belonging or origin is added. Many biblical names function this way: a termination is added to the name of the village or region from which the person comes. The meaning of the name Hittite itself might refer to the idea of "going out" or "going outside," but we know little about this place.
H8491.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:45, where it qualifies Jocha. This passage lists the valiant warriors who gathered around David at Ziklag, before he became king of Israel. Jocha is named as "the Hittite," indicating that he came from a specific locality, probably in Israel, although this place is not mentioned elsewhere in the Scriptures.

sens: The fresh juice that flows from crushed grapes, before fermentation or during fermentation
Young wine, shortly after its production
By extension, wine in general in lists of provisions and blessings
Symbol of abundance and divine blessing
The harvest of grapes and its transformation into drink
H8492.detail:
1. Must is the sweet juice that flows from grapes when they are crushed underfoot. It is a liquid in the process of transformation, naturally fermenting. Isaiah 65:8 speaks of the "juice" found in a cluster: this is the must, the fresh liquid of the fruit, before it fully becomes aged wine.

2. Must also refers to very young wine, shortly after pressing. At this stage, it still retains the flavor and color of fresh grapes. Hosea 4:11 lists it alongside wheat and oil as a central element of the people's food.

3. In lists of wealth and tributes (Deuteronomy 14:23, Nehemiah 13:12), must appears alongside wheat and oil as one of the three major products of the land of Israel. It is a way of saying "wine" in general, emphasizing its character as an abundant harvest.

4. Must embodies the material blessing that God pours out on His people. When Genesis 27:28 promises "wine in abundance," it is the promise of a generous land that, each year, offers its fruits at harvest time.

5. Symbolically, must represents vitality and joy: Joel 2:24 announces that the vats will overflow with must at the time of restoration. It is the image of a renewed life, prosperous, filled by God.
H8492.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "drawing" or "pressing," describing the act of harvesting and pressing. It is an ancient word specific to the Semitic agricultural world. Must appears as a concrete reality from the beginnings of Israelite civilization: it is a product that only fertile land can offer, hence its constant association with divine blessing. It is regularly found alongside two other agricultural treasures: wheat and oil.
H8492.emploi: The word must appears 38 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of the Law (Deuteronomy), royal history (Kings, Chronicles), and the prophets (Isaiah, Hosea, Joel). It appears in three types of contexts: first as an element of blessing — God promises must to the faithful (Genesis 27:28, Deuteronomy 11:14); then as part of revenues and taxes — must must be brought to the priests (Deuteronomy 18:4, Nehemiah 10:37); finally as a sign of desolation — its disappearance announces judgment (Isaiah 24:7, Joel 1:10). Must always symbolizes earthly abundance and the continuity of the people's life with God's generosity.
H8492.portee: For the Christian, must reminds us that God does not abandon His people to material needs: He provides food and drink, signs of His tenderness toward those who obey Him. Contemplating the cycle of the harvest invites gratitude: each year, God renews His goodness. Conversely, the loss of must warns that sin dries up the source of blessing. This humble word speaks of an embodied religion, which does not despise bread, wine, and oil, but recognizes them as gifts from the Father.

sens: Character from the tribe of Judah
H8493.detail: Tirja is a man from the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Scriptures. He is the son of Jehalléleel and the brother of Ziph, Zipha, and Asareel (1 Chronicles 4:16). He appears in a genealogy of descendants of Judah, with no specific actions or events reported concerning him in the Bible.
H8493.origine: The name "Tirja" literally means "fear" or "dread" in Hebrew. It comes from the root that expresses fear or reverence. Like many Hebrew names, it likely reflects a circumstance or feeling related to the time of this child's birth, or a parental wish for divine protection.
H8493.emploi: Tirja appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:16, in a genealogical list of descendants of Judah during the divided monarchy. His name simply appears among those of his brothers, with no specific account of events or actions in his life. He represents one of the many Judeans whose name has been preserved in the genealogical records of Israel.

sens: Son of Japheth and grandson of Noah
H8494.detail: Tiras is a biblical character mentioned at the time of humanity's origins after the flood. He is one of the seven sons of Japheth, who himself is one of the three sons of Noah. The name appears in the genealogical lists of Genesis and 1 Chronicles, always in the same positions: after Meshech and as the last son listed of Japheth (Genesis 10:2 and 1 Chronicles 1:5). These genealogical lists serve to establish the ancestors of the peoples who populated the earth after the flood.
H8494.origine: The name Tiras means "desire" in Hebrew. Like all the names of the sons of Japheth, it likely represents an ancient nation or people, although the precise historical identification of the people or territory it refers to is uncertain. It is a genealogical name marking direct descent in the post-flood lineage.
H8494.emploi: Tiras is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists: once in Genesis 10:2 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:5, which reiterates and confirms the same genealogy. He is listed among the sons of Japheth, alongside Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, and Meshech. No particular narrative concerns Tiras; he appears only in these enumerations of the nations descended from Noah.

sens: Animal: the male of the goat
Tribute or gift: animal offered as a present or tribute
Image of pride or lofty dignity
H8495.detail: 1. A buck is the adult male of the goat, distinguished from the female (doe) and the young (kid). It is a robust animal, useful for reproduction and for providing milk, meat, and leather. In Genesis 30:35, Jacob separates the spotted bucks from the other animals in his flock, as their color makes them remarkable. 2. Bucks are among the valuable goods offered as gifts or tribute. In Genesis 32:14, Jacob prepares a huge gift for his brother Esau, which includes twenty bucks among other animals. In 2 Chronicles 17:11, the peoples bring to Jehoshaphat a tribute including seven thousand seven hundred bucks, demonstrating the wealth and power of the king. 3. In Proverbs 30:31, the buck illustrates a majestic appearance and a confident stride: it is the very image of quiet pride, alongside the equipped horse or the king who fears no one.
H8495.origine: The Hebrew word תַּיִשׁ (tayish) has designated the male of the goat since antiquity. It belongs to the vocabulary of shepherds and herders in the Near East, where the goat was one of the most common domesticated animals. The root evokes the power and virility of the male breeder.
H8495.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate a concrete animal: bucks from the flock, gifts, or tributes. In Genesis 30 and 32, it refers to ordinary animals, counted and exchanged within a pastoral economy. In 2 Chronicles 17, the bucks testify to the wealth and international prestige of King Jehoshaphat. In Proverbs 30, the only passage where the buck is not listed among goods, it becomes a symbol, alongside the horse and the king, of a certain form of natural dignity and majesty.
H8495.portee: The buck reminds the reader that the Bible situates faith in the concrete aspects of daily life: herding, commerce, gifts, and tributes. It is also a lesson in sobriety: even the most ordinary domesticated animals can illustrate a spiritual truth. In Proverbs 30, the buck invites recognition of images of dignity and assurance in creation, reflecting the order that God has established.

sens: Deception or lie intended to mislead someone
Act of violence or injustice against a weak person
One who commits such acts
H8496.detail:
1. Fraud is primarily a deception, a lie spoken to deceive others. This is what the psalmist describes when he speaks of the mouth "full of curses, deceptions, and fraud" (Psalms 10:7): deceitful words that come from the mouth of the wicked. Similarly, in Psalms 55:12, fraud is added to deception as a weapon of the corrupt heart that fills the city.
2. Fraud also refers to oppression, that is, the act of unjustly dominating and exploiting the weak. The just king "will deliver" the unfortunate "from oppression and violence" (Psalms 72:14): he will free them from those who crush them by force or cunning.
3. The oppressor is one who commits these acts — who deceives or crushes. In Proverbs 29:13, "the poor and the oppressor meet," meaning that one who lives by fraud and violence encounters the poor he exploits.
H8496.origine: The Hebrew word tokh comes from a root that evokes the idea of breaking, shattering, or destroying. It primarily describes the physical or moral act of "breaking" another's trust, integrity, or peace. Fraud and oppression are assaults: one breaks sincerity through lies, one breaks freedom through violence. This is why this term encompasses both deception (which breaks trust) and oppression (which breaks dignity).
H8496.emploi: The word tokh appears 4 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Psalms and Proverbs. Three times it is rendered as "fraud": it refers to lies, deceitful words that fill the mouth or the places of the city (Psalms 10:7 and 55:12). Once it is translated as "oppression" (Psalms 72:14) and "oppressor" (Proverbs 29:13): it then designates the brutal act of domination over the weak. The contexts are always moral and social: fraud characterizes the wicked, oppression harms the innocent, and it is God's business to free the victims.
H8496.portee: This word reminds the reader that lying and oppression are serious sins. Fraud destroys trust and common peace; oppression crushes the vulnerable. The Bible affirms that God sees these acts, hates them, and liberates those who suffer from them. This calls the believer to hate fraud in all its forms and to defend the innocent against oppression.

sens: to be arranged, positioned in a place
to be gathered, assembled
to receive a word or teaching while remaining present
H8497.detail:
1. The word describes a physical position or arrangement: the saints stand, meaning they are arranged, ordered, positioned in a certain way near the one who speaks. It is the image of someone taking or occupying a stable place, getting into order.
2. The idea extends to a gathering: one who stands is not isolated but is part of an organized group, presented or assembled together. The saints standing at your feet suggests both proximity and order.
3. In the biblical context, standing thus goes hand in hand with receiving: one who stands close to the speaker is in a position to listen and receive his words, as shown in Deuteronomy 33:3 where this physical disposition accompanies the act of receiving divine teaching.
H8497.origine: The Hebrew תָּכָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of placing, arranging, or organizing. The Hebrew word used here belongs to the family of action verbs that describe an ordering or composition. Although its exact form is rare in the Bible, it refers to this fundamental notion of arrangement and stable position.
H8497.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 33:3. Moses, while blessing the tribes of Israel, speaks of God's love for the peoples and the holiness of those who serve Him. He says that the saints are in God's hand and that they stand at His feet to receive His words. The unique use of this word makes it a precious expression: it paints the image of an ordered, gathered, attentive, and receptive people to the divine word.
H8497.portee: This word shows us an important attitude of faith: that of standing, meaning taking a position of listening and receptivity before God. It is more than just physical presence; it is being arranged, gathered, and ready to receive divine teaching. For the Christian reader, this evokes the importance of humbly placing oneself before God to hear and welcome His word.

sens: arrangement, organization of space or elements
layout, structure of a building or object
